Toddlers do better when parents are not improvising every meal.

Make a plan for:
- breakfast,
- one easy lunch backup,
- a few grocery staples,
- where you go when everyone is tired.

Related: [Groceries, meals, routines in Bali](/guides/groceries-meals-routines-in-bali)

### 5) Parent regulation counts too

A toddler move gets shaky when adults are stretched.

The right setup often looks boring from the outside:
- one area,
- fewer commitments,
- a driver when needed,
- less bouncing around,
- more repeated rhythms.

That is not wasted Bali. That is how Bali becomes livable.

## The best move sequence with toddlers

1. **Start with a test stay** if you can.  
2. Pick **2–3 areas** that make short trips possible.  
3. Use the **budget calculator** with transport and convenience in mind.  
4. View housing only once you understand your daily loop.  
5. Add learning or activities only after the basic rhythm feels calm.

Use:
- [Test stay](/test-stay)
- [Budget calculator](/budget-calculator)
- [Settling in](/settling-in)

## When Empathy School matters in a toddler move

Not every toddler move starts with school.

But if you are considering Empathy School for early years or for an older sibling, it can still be useful to visit early.

Why?
Because the commute, the atmosphere, and the shape of the morning all affect where you live.

Start here:
- [Empathy School](/schools)
- [What to ask on a school tour](/guides/what-to-ask-on-a-school-tour)

## What to test during a toddler stay

Try to answer these before you commit to anything bigger:

- Which area made mornings feel easiest?
- How long did groceries really take?
- Could your toddler nap well in the home?
- What happened on a hot, tired, slightly chaotic day?
- Did the adults still have enough bandwidth by evening?

That last question matters more than people admit.

## A good-enough version of Bali with toddlers

A good toddler setup in Bali often looks like:
- one calm base,
- one main outing pattern,
- one food routine,
- one backup health plan,
- one or two weekly anchors.

You do not need the whole island.
You need a life you can repeat.

## Next steps

- [Family paths](/family-paths)
- [Bali areas for toddlers](/guides/bali-areas-for-toddlers)
- [Test stay](/test-stay)
- [Housing](/housing)
- [Settling in](/settling-in)

guides.title: What to ask a housing agent in Bali before you say yes
guides.description: A practical checklist for families: how to talk to a housing agent, what to verify, and which answers should make you slow down.

faqs.q: Should we use a housing agent in Bali?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Agents can save time, but they do not remove the need to verify contracts, ownership, pricing, and what is actually included.

faqs.q: What should we ask before the first viewing?
faqs.a: Ask about the area, length of lease, what is included, who manages repairs, and what the payment structure looks like.

faqs.q: What answer is a red flag?
faqs.a: Evasive answers about ownership, pressure to pay fast, changing stories, or reluctance to put details in writing.

faqs.q: Can we still use this if we are talking to Gaia Group?
faqs.a: Yes. These questions are here to help you stay clear-headed with any housing partner, including preferred partners.

guides.body:
## Quick take

A good housing agent should make the process clearer.

Not pushier. Not foggier. Clearer.

## Before the first call

Ask:
- Which areas do you think fit our family and why?
- What lease lengths do you usually help with?
- What’s typically included in the homes you show?
- How do you handle maintenance or repair questions?
- What documents should we expect before paying anything?

You are listening for clarity, not sales language.

## During the viewing process

Ask:
- Who owns this property?
- Who signed the listing off?
- What is included in the rent?
- What is not included?
- If we like it, what happens next?

Then ask the same questions again later in writing.

If the answers move around, take that seriously.

## Before any money changes hands

Ask:
- What is the deposit for?
- When is it returned?
- What can it be deducted for?
- What is the payment schedule?
- Will we receive a receipt?
- Who signs the agreement?

Related:
- [Lease + deposit checklist](/resources/lease-deposit-checklist)
- [Lease + deposit questions](/guides/lease-and-deposit-questions-in-bali)

## Questions about fit, not just paperwork

Families sometimes focus so hard on the contract that they skip the daily-life questions.

Ask:
- How noisy is this road at night?
- What do mornings feel like here?
- How far is the drive to Empathy School at real times?
- Where do families usually buy groceries nearby?
- What happens in rainy season?

Those answers matter just as much as the deposit clause.

## Red flags that should slow you down

- pressure to pay before you have documents,
- unclear ownership,
- “don’t worry about that” language,
- refusal to confirm details in writing,
- a price or story that changes mid-conversation,
- anything that relies on urgency more than clarity.

## What we learned the hard way

The best agents do not remove your responsibility.

They reduce the number of unknowns.

That is a much better standard.

## Next steps

- [Housing](/housing)
- [Housing viewing scorecard](/resources/housing-viewing-scorecard)
- [Renting safely in Bali](/guides/renting-safely-in-bali)

guides.title: Culture in Bali with kids (a respectful, calm approach)
guides.description: How families join cultural moments respectfully—what helped, what to ask locals, and what to watch out for.

video.title: CICAK CICAK (music video)
video.summary: A gentle cultural touchpoint for kids: a simple song in video form. Use it as a bridge—something children can enjoy—while you learn how culture shows up in daily life (and how to join respectfully).

faqs.q: Is this official advice?
faqs.a: No. It’s experience-based guidance. When in doubt, ask locals or your community guide and follow their lead.

faqs.q: Do we need to understand everything to participate respectfully?
faqs.a: Not at all. Start small: observe, ask, follow the flow, and prioritize respect over comprehension.

faqs.q: Should we film ceremonies for memories?
faqs.a: Ask first, keep filming minimal, and avoid close-ups of people. When in doubt, don’t film.

guides.body:
## A calm principle (so you don’t overthink it)

We’ve found the safest approach is:

- **be a respectful guest**,
- **ask locals what’s appropriate**,
- and **avoid turning culture into a performance**.

This guide is not a rulebook. Culture differs by village and context.

If you want a copy/paste version: [Culture with kids: quick checklist](/resources/culture-with-kids-quick-checklist).

---

## Quick start

- Start with **one** cultural touchpoint that’s easy for kids (song, language, small ritual).
- When invited to ceremonies, **ask first**: “Is it okay if we join/watch? Where should we stand?”
- Keep it short for children (snacks + water + exit plan).

---

## What “respectful participation” looks like in practice

### 1) Ask first (and accept “no” gracefully)

Simple scripts that work:
- “Is it okay for us to join?”
- “Where should we stand?”
- “Is it okay to take a photo?”

When you ask, you’re signaling you understand you’re a guest.

### 2) Dress and behavior

Families do best when they default to:
- modest clothing,
- calm, quiet voices,
- following the flow instead of improvising.

If you’re unsure about what’s expected, copy the checklist: [Culture with kids: quick checklist](/resources/culture-with-kids-quick-checklist).

### 3) Phones and filming

We’ve found the “lowest-risk” rule is:
- **ask first**,
- film less than you think,
- avoid close-ups of people,
- and put the phone away quickly.

### 4) Make it kid-friendly

Even culturally beautiful moments can be overwhelming for kids.

What helps:
- short duration,
- clear boundaries (“we’re watching quietly for 10 minutes”),
- a quiet exit plan,
- a gentle debrief after.

---

## Supporting social context (optional)

If you’d like a small example of culture/wellness moments families sometimes join, this reel is supporting context:

- Melukat reel: https://www.instagram.com/empathy.school/reel/DQdzsASEftg/

(Reminder: social is supporting context. The written guide is the primary answer.)

---

## What we learned the hard way

The mistake isn’t “not knowing enough.”

The mistake is **acting too confident**.

Humility works here. Asking works. Following works.

---

## A gentle next step

If your family is planning a move and wants the broader context:

- [Daily life](/daily-life)
- [Start here (roadmap)](/start-here)
- [Schools & learning](/schools)

guides.title: Finding community in Bali with kids (without forcing it)
guides.description: A parent-first way to help kids make friends and help adults feel less isolated—using repetition, routines, and low-pressure anchors.

video.title: Volunteering & community (a glimpse)
video.summary: A short glimpse of community volunteering at Empathy School. It’s not ‘the’ answer—just a reminder that community usually comes from repetition: same places, same faces, over a few weeks.

faqs.q: How long does it take to feel settled?
faqs.a: For many families, the shift happens around week 2–6—once kids have one routine and parents have seen the same people repeatedly.

faqs.q: Do we need to join a lot of groups?
faqs.a: Usually no. One or two consistent anchors beats five scattered attempts.

faqs.q: What’s the fastest ‘anchor’ for kids?
faqs.a: Often school pick-up, a short camp/weekly program, or a weekly class—anything with repeated contact and friendly adults.

guides.body:
## The principle (so you don’t overthink it)

Community in Bali is rarely a single discovery.

It’s usually built from **repetition**:

- same places,
- same times,
- same people,

…for long enough that everyone stops feeling like strangers.

---

## Quick start (week 1–2)

If you want your move to feel calmer quickly:

1) Pick **one child anchor** (school/camp/class) that happens weekly.
2) Pick **one parent anchor** (market/cafe/playground/co-working) you’ll repeat.
3) Keep it small for 2 weeks—then expand.

Useful companion:
- [First month setup checklist](/resources/first-month-setup-checklist)

---

## The 4 “community anchors” that work for most families

### 1) School pick-up (or camp pick-up)

Pick-up is community without pressure.
You’ll see the same parents, and conversations start naturally.

If you’re visiting first, camps can create the same effect:
- [Camps & short-term programs](/camps)

### 2) A weekly class/sport

Kids connect faster when there’s a shared activity.
Parents connect because you’re all waiting together.

### 3) A consistent “food routine”

One market or cafe you repeat becomes social faster than you expect.

Deep dive:
- [Groceries & meal routines](/guides/groceries-meals-routines-in-bali)

### 4) Volunteering (only if it fits your season)

Volunteering is optional.
But when it fits, it can accelerate belonging because you’re contributing, not consuming.

---

## Simple scripts that reduce awkwardness

These are low-pressure and usually welcomed:

- “Hi, we’re new—what area are you based in?”
- “Do you know any kid-friendly activities around here?”
- “We’re here for a few weeks—any tips for rainy afternoons?”

You don’t need to be extroverted. You just need to repeat the environment.

---

## What to watch out for (practical safety)

Most groups are lovely, but for family safety:

- Don’t overshare personal details early (address, school details, schedules).
- Prefer meeting in public spaces first.
- For services (nannies, drivers, rentals), use checklists and verify basics.

If your family is still deciding where to base yourselves, start here:
- [Where to live in Bali for families](/guides/where-to-live-in-bali-for-families)

---

## What we learned the hard way

The trap is trying a new thing every day.

Novelty feels productive, but it slows community.

Repetition feels boring—but it’s what creates belonging.

---

## Next steps

- [Daily life](/daily-life)
- [Start here (roadmap)](/start-here)
- [Schools & learning](/schools)
- [Camps & short-term programs](/camps)

guides.title: Bali areas for teens: how to choose
guides.description: How to shortlist Bali areas that support teens—connection, activities, independence, and a home base that can recharge.

faqs.q: Do teens get bored in quieter areas?
faqs.a: Some do, some don’t. It depends on whether they can plug into an activity community (sport, art, volunteering) quickly. If you choose a quieter base, plan the activity loop.

faqs.q: Is Canggu always best for teens?
faqs.a: Not always. Canggu offers a lot, but the busy feel and traffic can be a tradeoff. Some families prefer a calmer base and travel for activities.

faqs.q: How can we support independence safely?
faqs.a: Start with a transport plan (driver, trusted routes, clear check-ins), then expand freedom gradually once routines and relationships are in place.

faqs.q: What’s a good test-stay length for teens?
faqs.a: Two weeks is ideal if you can schedule a few activities and see what a “normal week” feels like.

faqs.q: Should we choose location based on school?
faqs.a: School commutes matter a lot. If a school is part of your plan, treat commute time as a first-class decision factor.

guides.body:
## Quick take

With teens, the “best” area is usually the one that supports:

- independence (safe places to go)
- social connection (community + activities)
- reliable routines (school/learning, sports, clubs)
- family sanity (commutes and traffic are still real)

This guide gives you a way to shortlist 2–3 areas for a test stay and tours — without pretending there’s one perfect answer.

## What matters most for teens

### 1) Connection (they need “their people”)
Teens do better when they can quickly find:
- a sport or club
- a creative community
- a group they can join consistently

Ask: **“Where will my teen make friends within 2–4 weeks?”**

### 2) Safe independence
Independence in Bali looks different. For many families it means:
- being able to go to a class or café with supervision nearby
- being able to move around with a driver or trusted transport plan
- walking short distances safely (depends heavily on the street)

### 3) Activity density
Teens need options. Areas with more:
- gyms, surf, art, music
- community spaces
- after-school programs
…often reduce “I’m bored” friction.

### 4) Home environment (noise + recovery)
Teens need quiet to decompress too. The right area balances:
- social opportunities
- a home base that can be calm enough to recharge

## Areas that often fit teens (with tradeoffs)

### Canggu / Berawa / Pererenan
High activity density and a lot of teen-relevant options.
Tradeoffs: traffic and the “busy” feel can drain some families.
Explore: [/areas/canggu](/areas/canggu), [/areas/berawa](/areas/berawa), [/areas/pererenan](/areas/pererenan)

### Seminyak / Kerobokan
Strong “services + activity” base.
Tradeoffs: can feel more adult-oriented and busier in parts.
Explore: [/areas/seminyak](/areas/seminyak), [/areas/kerobokan](/areas/kerobokan)

### Sanur (routine + sport)
Often calmer but still has activity options and a stable routine vibe.
Tradeoffs: less “buzz” than Canggu; your teen may want more variety.
Explore: [/areas/sanur](/areas/sanur)

### Ubud (creative + nature)
Great for creative teens, nature-loving families, and deeper community.
Tradeoffs: rainy season routines, and some teens miss the beach buzz.
Explore: [/areas/ubud](/areas/ubud)

## Checklist: teen test-stay questions

- Where will they go 3 times a week? (sport, art, club, volunteering)
- What’s the transport plan that feels safe for us?
- Where can they hang out in a healthy way?
- Is the home base calm enough to recharge?
- Are we okay with the activity level of the area long-term?

## Next steps

- If you’re deciding where to live: [/areas](/areas)
- If you want a “family logistics” plan: [/guides/family-transport-drivers-scooters-cars](/guides/family-transport-drivers-scooters-cars)
- If you’re just starting: [/start-here](/start-here)

guides.title: Bali areas for toddlers: how to choose
guides.description: A parent-first way to shortlist Bali areas that work well with toddler routines—commutes, naps, heat, and daily life.

faqs.q: Do we need to be close to the beach for toddlers?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many toddler routines work best with shade, predictable errands, and a few repeatable activities. Beach access is a bonus if it fits your daily loop.

faqs.q: Is Ubud too far from services?
faqs.a: Ubud has plenty of day-to-day services, but travel time can still surprise you depending on exactly where you live. Choose a location that keeps your routine easy, and test-stay first.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest mistake families make with toddlers?
faqs.a: Choosing an area for the “Instagram vibe” and then realizing daily errands are too slow or stressful. Your routine is the product—optimize for that.

faqs.q: How long should our test stay be?
faqs.a: 10–14 days is usually enough to see traffic patterns, groceries, nap timing, and how the area feels on weekdays vs weekends.

faqs.q: Should we hire a driver right away?
faqs.a: Many families do, at least during the first month, to reduce stress while you learn routes and routines. It can also help you explore different areas safely.

guides.body:
## Quick take

With toddlers, the “best” area is usually the one that makes **daily life predictable**:

- Short trips (nap windows + traffic don’t mix)
- Easy access to basics (groceries, a clinic, a quiet café/park, a kids activity)
- A home that stays cool enough for naps
- A routine you can repeat even when you’re new

This guide helps you shortlist 2–3 areas for a **test stay** — not “pick the perfect forever neighborhood.”

## What matters most for toddlers

### 1) Commute and nap math
If a typical errand turns into a 45–60 minute ride, it affects everything:
- nap timing
- snack timing
- parent patience
- the ability to say “yes” to small outings

**Rule of thumb:** choose an area where your daily loop (home → groceries → activity → home) is realistically doable.

### 2) Shade, heat, and walkability
You don’t need a “walkable city,” but you do want:
- shaded paths where possible
- places you can pop into with a stroller
- safe, short “outdoor resets” (even 15 minutes matters)

### 3) Medical access and “backup plans”
Most toddler stress comes from “what if” moments:
- fever at night
- falls and bumps
- stomach bugs
- rash / allergy surprises

Choose an area where you can answer: **“What’s our plan if we need help today?”**

### 4) Community + routines
Toddlers thrive when parents have support:
- other families nearby
- playgroups or simple activities
- predictable food + groceries

## A simple shortlist method (10 minutes)

Pick 2–3 areas where you can say “yes” to all three:

1) **We can keep our routine.** (sleep / meals / calm time)  
2) **We can get help quickly.** (clinic + basic services)  
3) **We can leave the house easily.** (short outings without “traffic dread”)

Then do a **test stay** for 10–14 days before you commit to longer-term housing.

## Areas that often fit toddlers (with tradeoffs)

These are *common* toddler-friendly fits. Your exact street matters a lot.

### Sanur
- Often feels calmer and more routine-friendly
- Easier “family loop” day-to-day
- Tradeoff: nightlife is quieter; some families find it “too calm” after a few months  
Explore: [/areas/sanur](/areas/sanur)

### Ubud
- Nature, slower pace, lots of kid-friendly classes and community
- Tradeoff: humidity, rain patterns, and some roads can be slower than you expect  
Explore: [/areas/ubud](/areas/ubud)

### Renon / Denpasar (family base option)
- More “city practical” for appointments and services
- Tradeoff: not a beach/nature vibe; you’ll drive for weekend scenery  
Explore: [/areas/renon](/areas/renon) and [/areas/denpasar](/areas/denpasar)

### Jimbaran / Nusa Dua (resort-adjacent routine)
- Often predictable, quieter, and easier for beach days
- Tradeoff: it can feel “spread out” and car-dependent  
Explore: [/areas/jimbaran](/areas/jimbaran) and [/areas/nusa-dua](/areas/nusa-dua)

## Areas to approach carefully (not “bad,” just plan for reality)

### Canggu / Berawa / Pererenan
These can work beautifully — but traffic and noise can be real.

If you’re considering them, do a test stay and ask:
- “Can we do groceries and one activity without losing the whole day?”
- “Are we okay with scooters around our daily route?”
Explore: [/areas/canggu](/areas/canggu), [/areas/berawa](/areas/berawa), [/areas/pererenan](/areas/pererenan)

### Seminyak / Kerobokan
Great access to restaurants and services, but can feel busy.
Explore: [/areas/seminyak](/areas/seminyak), [/areas/kerobokan](/areas/kerobokan)

## Checklist: toddler test-stay questions

Copy/paste this into your notes:

- Where is the closest clinic we’d actually use?
- How long is groceries → home at 5pm?
- Where do we go for a 30-minute “reset” outside?
- Is our home cool enough for naps?
- Can we find familiar foods quickly?
- What’s our rainy-day activity plan?

## Next steps

- If you haven’t yet: start with the family roadmap: [/start-here](/start-here)
- Compare a few areas quickly: [/areas](/areas)
- Then plan a test stay: [/guides/two-week-test-stay-plan](/guides/two-week-test-stay-plan)

guides.title: Bali arrival checklist (eVOA, Arrival Card, tourist levy)
guides.description: A parent-friendly checklist for landing days—what to do before you fly, what to do at the airport, and what to double-check using official sources.

faqs.q: Do we need to do anything online before we fly?
faqs.a: Often yes. The safest approach is to check the official portals (eVisa/e‑VOA, arrival card, levy) and your airline requirements right before travel, because steps and fees can change.

faqs.q: Should we pay the tourist levy in advance?
faqs.a: If you choose to, use the official levy site. If you don’t, keep a note to do it shortly after arrival and save your proof of payment.

faqs.q: Where can we confirm the current steps?
faqs.a: Use the official links list and confirm with your airline or a trusted agent for your exact passport situation.

guides.body:
## Quick start (the calm version)

1. Bookmark **Official links**: [/official-links](/official-links)  
2. Prepare a **single “arrival folder”** (digital + printed): passports, return/onward, accommodation, insurance, kids’ documents.  
3. Decide your airport plan: **stroller**, **snacks**, **bathroom strategy**, **SIM plan**, **cash plan**.  
4. After landing: go slow, hydrate, and keep everything in one bag until you’re through.

> Safety note: we share experience and checklists — not legal or immigration advice. Rules change.

## Before you fly (24–72 hours)

### 1) Confirm the current entry steps
- Open: [/official-links](/official-links)
- Check:
  - eVisa / e‑VOA portal
  - Arrival Card portal
  - Bali tourist levy portal
- If anything looks different than you expected, **pause** and verify (airline + official portal + your agent if you’re using one).

### 2) Build a family “arrival folder”
We keep one folder with:
- Passports (and copies)
- Any visa/approval documents (if applicable)
- Proof of accommodation
- Return/onward booking proof (if applicable)
- Travel/health insurance info (if applicable)
- Kids’ documents (birth certificate scans, school letters if relevant)
- Emergency contacts

### 3) Plan for first-night energy levels
A good landing plan assumes:
- kids are hungry at the wrong time
- everyone needs bathrooms at the same time
- one bag will get searched (so don’t bury essentials)

## Landing day (airport checklist)

### Step 1: Get through the airport calmly
- Keep passports + essential documents in **one pouch**
- Use a simple queue rule: “one adult holds documents, one adult manages kids”
- If you’re traveling with multiple children, decide *ahead of time* who stays with bags

### Step 2: SIM / connectivity plan
Choose one:
- Get a SIM/eSIM before travel (less stress at the airport)
- Get connected after you arrive (fine, but plan for a short “offline window”)

Related guide: [Phones and internet in Bali](/guides/phones-and-internet-in-bali)

### Step 3: Cash + payments
Have at least a small amount of IDR for:
- snacks/water
- small fees
- taxis (if needed)

Related guide: [Banking & payments in Bali](/guides/banking-payments-in-bali)

### Step 4: Your first transport decision
For a family arrival, we usually plan one of these:
- pre-arranged driver pickup (lowest stress)
- reputable taxi / ride-hail (good backup)

Related guide: [Family transport in Bali: drivers, scooters, cars](/guides/family-transport-drivers-scooters-cars)

## After you arrive (first 48 hours)

### A) Do a “settle” day
Before you start admin tasks:
- rest
- hydrate
- groceries
- simple meal
- early bedtime

### B) Do the minimum setup tasks
Use this checklist: [First week setup checklist](/guides/first-week-in-bali-setup-checklist)

## What we learned the hard way
When you’re tired, you’re vulnerable to mistakes. The best arrival plan is the one that **assumes you’re not thinking clearly** and keeps decisions simple.

## Next good reads
- [Start here: parent-first roadmap](/start-here)
- [Visa scam red flags](/guides/visa-scam-red-flags)
- [Renting safely in Bali](/guides/renting-safely-in-bali)

guides.title: Bali safety basics for families (practical, not scary)
guides.description: A parent-first safety checklist: traffic, water, sun, mosquitoes, and “small habits” that reduce risk without turning life into fear.

faqs.q: Is Bali safe for kids?
faqs.a: Many families live here happily, but safety comes from habits: traffic awareness, sun protection, and good water/food practices.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest day-to-day risk for families?
faqs.a: For many families it’s road safety. The “small risk” tasks add up: crossings, scooters, night driving, and fatigue.

faqs.q: How do we avoid overthinking safety?
faqs.a: Pick a few high-impact habits (helmets, hydration, mosquito plan, safe swimming rules) and stick to them consistently.

guides.body:
## Quick start (high-impact habits)
- Treat **road safety** as the main daily risk.
- Make a **mosquito plan** (especially at dusk).
- Build a **sun + hydration** routine.
- Choose safe swimming spots and follow “two adult eyes” rules for young kids.

## 1) Road safety (the big one)
- Assume traffic is unpredictable.
- Avoid late-night driving when you’re tired.
- If you use scooters, treat helmets as non‑negotiable.
- For school tours and early weeks, many families use drivers.

Guide: [Family transport options](/guides/family-transport-drivers-scooters-cars)

## 2) Water and food (simple rules)
We don’t try to be perfect — we aim for consistency:
- drink safe water (ask your accommodation what they provide)
- wash hands before meals (especially after playgrounds)
- keep snacks on hand so kids don’t “crash” into street food choices

## 3) Sun and heat
- hats + sunscreen becomes part of leaving the house
- plan “midday quiet time” when possible
- keep electrolytes on hand for active days

## 4) Mosquitoes (especially evenings)
A practical routine:
- long sleeves at dusk when possible
- repellant where appropriate
- reduce standing water around your home
- if you’re worried, ask a local clinic for the most current guidance

Guide: [Healthcare in Bali for families](/guides/healthcare-in-bali-for-families)

## 5) Swimming and ocean
- Choose beaches with safer conditions for kids (ask locals)
- When in doubt: pool day > risky surf day
- “Two adult eyes” for young kids

## What we learned the hard way
The goal isn’t “zero risk.” It’s building a calm set of habits that reduce risk without taking joy away.

## Next steps
- [Start here](/start-here)
- [Healthcare + emergencies](/guides/healthcare-in-bali-for-families)
- [Areas that feel calmer for families](/areas)

guides.title: Banking & payments in Bali (cards, cash, and the calm approach)
guides.description: A practical money setup for families: what to decide before you arrive, how to reduce fees, and how to avoid “we can’t pay” moments.

faqs.q: Do we need to carry cash in Bali?
faqs.a: Often yes for small purchases and in some locations. Many families use a mix of cards and cash depending on the area.

faqs.q: How do we avoid fees?
faqs.a: Fee structures vary by bank and card. The simplest strategy is to compare your bank’s fees ahead of time and keep a backup card.

faqs.q: What’s the easiest “first week” plan?
faqs.a: Arrive with a small amount of cash, have at least two ways to pay (two cards or card + backup), then refine once you know your routines.

guides.body:
## Quick take

The goal is not to build a perfect financial system on day one. It is to make everyday payments, deposits, and admin feel stable enough that money does not become a constant source of friction.

## What families usually need first

### A dependable way to pay immediately
Cards, cash, and one clear backup matter more than sophistication in the first days.

### A way to track commitments
Keep receipts, screenshots, and due dates for housing, school, transport, and short-stay costs in one place.

### A low-drama transfer habit
Large or important payments should feel documented and deliberate, not impulsive and chat-driven.

## Good first-week habits

- Photograph receipts that matter.
- Keep a note of recurring commitments and due dates.
- Confirm the name and details of the receiving party before higher-stakes transfers.
- Separate “daily spend” from “move commitments” so the month stays legible.

## What makes family budgeting easier

The move feels calmer when parents can answer:

- what has been paid,
- what is still due,
- what is refundable,
- and what belongs to setup rather than ordinary monthly life.

## Pair this with

- [Costs](/costs)
- [Budget calculator](/budget-calculator)
- [Arrival folder checklist](/resources/arrival-folder-checklist)

guides.title: Cost of living in Bali for families: a decision framework
guides.description: A budgeting framework that explains why costs vary—and how to compare options without guessing.
guides.body:
## Quick take

A Bali budget becomes useful when it stops pretending to be one exact number and starts behaving like a **decision framework**.

## The main drivers

### Housing
Housing changes the most when area, home style, and commute tolerance change. Rent by itself rarely tells the whole story.

### Learning
For this hub, the school question means Empathy School, camps, or short-term learning support that helps the family week work. Education can become one of the biggest swing factors quickly.

### Transport
A cheaper home can become a heavier month if it creates longer drives, more driver time, or more daily friction.

### Daily-life defaults
Food, childcare support, activities, and how often you “solve tiredness with spending” all affect the real budget.

## Use a three-layer range

### Low
The version of Bali that works if you keep the week simple and consciously reduce extras.

### Mid
The version most families actually want to live, once convenience and breathing room both matter.

### High
The version that protects more comfort, buffer, or support — and helps you see whether the move still feels worth it.

## Do not forget the setup month

The first month is often more expensive because it includes:

- deposits,
- short stays or overlapping stays,
- local setup purchases,
- transport experiments,
- and the cost of not yet knowing the easiest defaults.

## The best budget question

Instead of asking “What does Bali cost?” ask:

**What would our week cost in this area, with this housing style, with this amount of school / camp / transport friction?**

That question is slower, but it leads to better decisions.

## Next steps

- [Budget calculator](/budget-calculator)
- [Family budget range planner](/resources/family-budget-range-planner)
- [Housing style compare](/housing-style-compare)

guides.title: Family transport in Bali (drivers, scooters, cars)
guides.description: A calm, safety-first way to think about transport with kids: when scooters make sense, when they don’t, and how many families use drivers or cars.

faqs.q: Do families use scooters in Bali?
faqs.a: Some do, especially with older kids, but many families avoid scooters early on until they understand the roads and their own risk tolerance.

faqs.q: Is hiring a driver common?
faqs.a: Yes. Many families use a driver for airport trips, school runs, and long distances, especially when they’re new.

faqs.q: What’s the lowest-stress option for the first month?
faqs.a: Often a mix: walk where you can, use a driver for longer trips, and only add scooters once you feel confident and have the right gear.

guides.body:
## Quick start
- For your first month, prioritize **low-stress, low-risk** transport.
- Treat scooters as a *choice*, not a default.
- If you’re arriving soon: [Bali arrival checklist](/guides/bali-arrival-checklist-evoa-arrival-card-levy)

## Option 1: Walkable living (the best “transport hack”)
If you can choose an area where:
- groceries are close
- kids’ activities are close
- you can do “small life” without commuting

…your transport stress drops dramatically.

Start with: [Bali areas for families](/areas)

## Option 2: Driver (especially for new families)
A driver can help you:
- get from airport to accommodation calmly
- do housing viewings without chaos
- manage school runs (even short-term tours)

### What to ask a driver
- Are you available at school-run times?
- What’s your preferred communication method?
- What’s your policy if plans change?
- How do you handle car seats (if needed)?

> We avoid listing prices here because they change. Ask a few drivers or agencies and compare reliability and communication first.

## Option 3: Car (control + comfort, higher admin)
A car can be great for:
- multiple kids
- sports gear
- rainy season
…but it adds:
- parking stress in some areas
- maintenance/admin

## Option 4: Scooters (high freedom, higher risk)
Scooters can be practical when:
- you’re confident riding
- you understand local traffic patterns
- you’re strict about helmets and safe habits

Scooters are *not* for everyone, especially in the first weeks. It’s okay to decide “not for us.”

## What we learned the hard way
Transport choices quietly shape your whole Bali experience. If commuting feels stressful, even a perfect villa can stop feeling perfect.

## Related reads
- [Safety basics for families](/guides/bali-safety-basics-for-families)
- [Rainy season with kids](/blog/rainy-season-with-kids)
- [Where to live in Bali](/guides/where-to-live-in-bali-for-families)

guides.title: Groceries & meal routines in Bali (family-friendly)
guides.description: A parent-first approach to feeding your family in Bali: groceries, meal planning, and how to reduce decision fatigue when you’re new.

faqs.q: Is it easy to find familiar groceries?
faqs.a: Many families can find what they need, but availability varies by area. Expect some adaptation and keep a few “safe meals.”

faqs.q: What’s the simplest routine for the first week?
faqs.a: Pick 3–5 repeat meals, keep easy snacks, and avoid trying every new option at once.

faqs.q: How do we avoid spending too much on food?
faqs.a: A routine helps. Eating out constantly can creep up quickly. Mix home meals with a few reliable places.

guides.body:
## Quick start (reduce decision fatigue) - Choose **3 repeat breakfasts** and **3 repeat dinners** for your first week. - Keep a “safe snack bag” for outings. - Build one reliable grocery shop route in your area. ## Step 1: Decide your family food baseline Write down: - your kids’ “safe meals” - any allergies / sensitivities - your weekly rhythm (busy nights vs calm nights) ## Step 2: Do one “baseline shop” Buy: - breakfast basics - snack basics - simple proteins - easy veggies/fruits ## Step 3: Add variety slowly Once routine feels easy: - add new cafes or markets - add new recipes - add new snacks --- ## Markets and the “Bali rhythm” For many families, Bali starts feeling like home when you have: - one reliable grocery shop, - one market you repeat, - and a few default meals. Supporting reel (optional context):
If you want a kid-friendly activity that also supports routine, cooking classes can be a nice “anchor.” Supporting reel: https://www.instagram.com/empathy.school/reel/CzdBEPXvpA-/ ## What we learned the hard way When you’re new, food choices feel like constant decision-making. Routines buy you calm. ## Related reads - [Family transport](/guides/family-transport-drivers-scooters-cars) - [Areas for families](/areas) - [Cost of living framework](/guides/cost-of-living-for-families-framework) - [Daily life](/daily-life)

guides.title: Health insurance in Bali for families (how to choose coverage)
guides.description: A practical framework for families: what questions to ask, what to confirm in writing, and how to avoid buying the wrong thing for your reality.

faqs.q: Do we need insurance to live in Bali?
faqs.a: Needs vary by visa type, budget, and risk tolerance. Many families choose coverage for peace of mind and to reduce “what if” stress.

faqs.q: What should we confirm before buying a policy?
faqs.a: Confirm what counts as an emergency, which hospitals/clinics are included, and how claims work (direct billing vs reimbursement).

faqs.q: Where should we get medical guidance?
faqs.a: Use trusted clinics/hospitals for medical decisions. This page is a planning framework, not medical advice.

guides.body:
## Quick start
- Decide your “comfort goal”: *catastrophic coverage*, *routine coverage*, or *full-service peace of mind*.
- Confirm in writing:
  - what’s covered
  - how claims work
  - where you can go for care
- Don’t buy coverage you don’t understand.

Related: [Healthcare in Bali for families](/guides/healthcare-in-bali-for-families)

## Step 1: Choose the type of coverage you actually want
### A) Catastrophic-only
Good if:
- you can self-fund routine visits
- you mainly want protection from big surprises

### B) Routine + emergency
Good if:
- you expect regular clinic visits with kids
- you want predictable costs

### C) Premium peace of mind
Good if:
- you want direct billing options
- you want broader support (and accept higher cost)

## Step 2: Ask these questions (copy/paste)
1. What is the deductible and how does it apply?
2. Is dental included? Vision?
3. What counts as an emergency?
4. Do you reimburse or direct bill (and where)?
5. How do you handle pre-existing conditions?
6. What’s excluded in writing?

## Step 3: Pair insurance with a clinic plan
Even with insurance, it helps to decide:
- which clinic you’ll use for routine care
- where you’d go in an emergency

Guide: [Healthcare in Bali for families](/guides/healthcare-in-bali-for-families)

## What we learned the hard way
The right policy is the one that matches your real behavior. If you won’t file reimbursements, don’t buy a plan that relies on reimbursements.

## Next steps
- [Costs & logistics pillar](/costs)
- [Safety basics](/guides/bali-safety-basics-for-families)
- [Ask a question](/contact?topic=health)

guides.title: Healthcare in Bali for families: mindset + practical planning
guides.description: How families typically think about clinics, emergencies, and insurance—without pretending to be medical authorities.
guides.body:
## Quick take

This page is not medical advice. It is a planning page for families who want to avoid making healthcare decisions for the first time when everyone is already stressed.

## The three decisions that make healthcare calmer

### 1. Where do we go for small things?
Pick a likely clinic or provider for the low-drama problems: fever, stomach bugs, minor infections, or questions that need reassurance more than crisis response.

### 2. What is our emergency plan?
Decide who you would contact, how you would travel, and what information you would want immediately available if the problem feels urgent.

### 3. What paperwork do we need ready?
Keep copies of passports, insurance details, allergy notes, medications, and a short family medical summary where both adults can find it quickly.

## What to prepare before you need it

- Save local clinic / hospital details in both adults’ phones.
- Keep a small go-bag mindset for an unplanned appointment: water, snacks, wipes, change of clothes, charger.
- Know what your child’s baseline looks like when they are tired, dehydrated, or overstimulated so you do not lose time second-guessing yourself.

## The family version of “healthcare readiness”

Calm families usually have three things ready:

- a first move for non-emergency illness,
- a first move for urgent questions,
- and a way to reduce chaos while they decide which lane applies.

That may be as simple as one clinic, one emergency note, and one adult taking the admin lead while the other stays with the child.

## What catches families off guard

- small illnesses feeling bigger because transport is unfamiliar,
- not having insurance or ID details handy,
- assuming tired, overheated, or dehydrated children are only “off” when they may need closer attention.

## Pair this with

- [Health insurance in Bali for families](/guides/health-insurance-in-bali-for-families)
- [Sick-day plan for Bali families](/resources/sick-day-plan-for-bali-families)
- [Settling in](/settling-in)

guides.title: How to choose a visa agent in Bali (family checklist)
guides.description: A practical checklist for choosing a visa agent safely—what to ask, what to verify, and what red flags look like.

faqs.q: Should we only use the cheapest agent?
faqs.a: Price matters, but clarity matters more. Look for transparent fees, clear timelines, and consistent communication.

faqs.q: Do you recommend a single agent?
faqs.a: We may introduce families to partners we’ve vetted, but you should still use this checklist and compare options.

guides.body:
## Quick take

Most families don’t need the “perfect” visa agent. They need someone who is **clear**, **consistent**, and **honest about uncertainty**.

If an agent communicates well, gives you a checklist, and explains what could go wrong (without drama), that’s usually a better sign than flashy marketing.

## The family checklist

### Ask these questions

- What visa pathway are you recommending, and **why** for our situation?
- What documents do you need from us **before** you start?
- What’s the full fee breakdown (agent fee + government fees + extras)?
- What is the **realistic** timeline—and what commonly causes delays?
- How will you communicate updates (WhatsApp, email) and how often?

### Verify these things

- Their business presence is consistent (same name, same details across channels).
- They use official portals for the parts that require them.
- They provide a written summary (even a simple message) of fees + timeline.

### Prefer agents who say…

- “In our experience…”
- “Rules change—here’s the official link…”
- “We can’t guarantee outcomes, but here’s what we’ll do if it gets stuck.”

## What to avoid

- “Guaranteed approval.”
- Pressure to pay immediately without a written scope.
- Vague fees (“depends” without ranges or examples).

## Official sources

Keep these bookmarked so you’re never relying on memory: see [Official links](/official-links).

## Next steps

- Read [Visa scam red flags](/guides/visa-scam-red-flags)
- Go back to the overview: [Visas](/visas)

guides.title: Lease and deposit questions to ask in Bali (before you pay)
guides.description: A practical checklist for families: what to confirm in writing before paying a deposit or signing a lease, and which details cause the most stress later.

faqs.q: Is it normal to pay a deposit?
faqs.a: Deposits are common, but the key is clarity: what it covers, when it’s returned, and what counts as “damage.”

faqs.q: What should we insist on in writing?
faqs.a: Payment schedule, what’s included, maintenance responsibilities, and the exact conditions for returning the deposit.

faqs.q: Should we pay before seeing the property?
faqs.a: Be very cautious with payments before a viewing or a verified agreement. If something feels rushed, slow it down and verify.

guides.body:
## Quick take

Deposit stress is rarely about the money alone. It is about whether the terms, condition, and expectations were ever made clear enough in the first place.

## Questions worth asking before money moves

### What exactly is the deposit for?
Clarify what it covers, what could reduce it, and what happens if a plan changes.

### What condition is the home expected to be returned in?
Take photos, note existing issues, and keep a shared record.

### What sits inside maintenance and what does not?
Small repairs, equipment issues, internet problems, and appliance questions should not be left vague.

### What happens around notice, extension, or early exit?
Even if you do not expect changes, the terms matter more once family plans shift.

## A calmer way to handle it

- Keep the written terms together.
- Photograph the move-in state.
- Repeat your understanding back in writing.
- Slow down if the answers stay fuzzy.

## Pair this with

- [Renting safely in Bali](/guides/renting-safely-in-bali)
- [Lease deposit checklist](/resources/lease-deposit-checklist)
- [Housing viewing scorecard](/resources/housing-viewing-scorecard)

guides.title: Packing list for Bali with kids (what we’d bring again)
guides.description: A practical packing guide for families relocating or test-staying in Bali—what’s easy to buy locally and what’s worth bringing.

faqs.q: Can we buy most things in Bali?
faqs.a: Many basics are available, but specific brands or specialty items may be harder to find depending on the area. For a test stay, pack for comfort and simplicity.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest packing mistake?
faqs.a: Packing for “every scenario.” Prioritize what reduces stress in your first month: sleep, sun/heat, and routines.

faqs.q: Should we bring school supplies?
faqs.a: Some families bring a small starter set, then buy locally once they know what their school expects.

guides.body:
## Quick take

Most families do better when they pack for the **first week**, not for every possible Bali scenario.

## Pack first for function

### Carry-on essentials
- passports and entry documents,
- one change of clothes per child,
- medicines you really use,
- chargers, comfort item, snacks, and anything that protects the first tired evening.

### First-week basics
- lightweight clothes that can repeat,
- simple rain layer,
- sun protection,
- sandals or shoes that can get wet,
- swimwear only if it supports your real week, not just the fantasy version.

### Child regulation items
Bring the small familiar things that help your child reset: headphones, preferred cup, bedtime object, one book, one easy activity.

## Things families often overpack

- too many “just in case” outfits,
- bulky toys instead of a few reliable comfort objects,
- items they could easily buy after arrival.

## What is worth protecting

The smartest packing list protects:

- sleep,
- first-day hydration and meals,
- basic health needs,
- and emotional familiarity for the children.

## Use this with

- [First week in Bali setup checklist](/guides/first-week-in-bali-setup-checklist)
- [First-week arrival checklist](/resources/first-week-arrival-checklist)
- [Daily life](/daily-life)

guides.title: Phones and internet in Bali (a family setup guide)
guides.description: A simple connectivity plan for families: how to avoid landing-day stress, what to set up first, and what to test before you rely on it.

faqs.q: Should we get an eSIM before we arrive?
faqs.a: If you want less stress on landing day, yes. If you’re comfortable being offline for a few hours, you can do it after arrival.

faqs.q: What’s the first thing to test in a new accommodation?
faqs.a: Internet reliability. Test speed and stability at the times you’ll actually use it (morning work blocks and evening streaming).

faqs.q: Do we need a local phone number?
faqs.a: Many families find it helpful for deliveries, appointments, and day-to-day coordination.

guides.body:
## Quick take

Sort connectivity early. It quietly affects transport, payments, school communication, work calls, food delivery, maps, and how calm the adults stay.

## The three layers to protect

### Arrival connection
Have a way to get online as soon as possible after landing so the first hours are not guesswork.

### Daily phone reliability
Make sure the adults can message, navigate, pay, and coordinate child-related logistics without dependence on one fragile setup.

### Home or work-grade backup
If remote work matters, treat home internet and a backup option as part of your housing and area decision, not an afterthought.

## Best first moves

- confirm how both adults will stay reachable,
- test maps and messaging before the first heavy day,
- keep key addresses, drivers, and school contacts easy to access,
- do not rely on “we’ll figure it out if the internet drops” if work or school makes that risky.

## What families underestimate

Connectivity is not only about work. It is also about how fast a tired, hot, lost, or sick day escalates when one phone plan fails.

## Next steps

- [Weekday Reality](/weekday-reality)
- [Housing](/housing)
- [Arrival folder checklist](/resources/arrival-folder-checklist)

guides.title: Quiet + nature areas in Bali: how to choose
guides.description: A calm, realistic guide to choosing a quiet base in Bali—without accidentally isolating your family from services and community.

faqs.q: Is Ubud always quiet?
faqs.a: Ubud varies by micro-area. Some streets are calm and green; others are busy. A short test stay helps you feel the difference.

faqs.q: Will we feel isolated in a quiet area?
faqs.a: It depends on whether you build a weekly rhythm and community touchpoints. Quiet works best with intentional connection.

faqs.q: Do we need a car in quieter areas?
faqs.a: Often yes, or at least a driver plan. The quieter the area, the more you’ll likely plan transport for errands and activities.

faqs.q: What’s the best quiet beach area?
faqs.a: It depends on your definition of quiet and how close you want services. Some families like calmer coastal pockets while still staying within reach of larger hubs.

faqs.q: How do we avoid choosing ‘too quiet’?
faqs.a: Decide what services you want within 10–15 minutes, then shortlist areas that can realistically support that. Quiet shouldn’t mean constant inconvenience.

guides.body:
## Quick take

If your family wants **quiet + nature** (and you’re okay with fewer “city conveniences”), Bali can be amazing.

But “quiet” is not a single place — it’s a set of tradeoffs:
- less noise, fewer crowds
- more intentional routines
- sometimes longer trips for services

This guide helps you choose a quiet base without accidentally isolating yourself.

## Define what “quiet” means for your family

Quiet can mean:
- less traffic and fewer scooters
- a home base with green views
- fewer nightlife distractions
- cooler evenings (depends on elevation and breeze)

Write down your top two:
1) ______________  
2) ______________

## Areas that often suit quiet + nature (with tradeoffs)

### Sidemen
Deep nature, slower pace, and a “reset” feeling.
Tradeoff: fewer services; you’ll plan errands more intentionally.
Explore: [/areas/sidemen](/areas/sidemen)

### Ubud (choose your micro-area carefully)
Ubud can be calm and green — but some parts are busy.
Tradeoff: rainy season routines and tourist density in certain pockets.
Explore: [/areas/ubud](/areas/ubud)

### Amed
Coastal quiet, simple life, and space to breathe.
Tradeoff: distance to some services; best for families who truly want slow.
Explore: [/areas/amed](/areas/amed)

### Seseh (calmer coastal feel)
Often calmer than central Canggu areas while still being “not too far.”
Tradeoff: you’ll still have traffic moments depending on your route.
Explore: [/areas/seseh](/areas/seseh)

## Checklist: “quiet base” reality checks

- What are we willing to drive for weekly?
- How often do we need bigger services (medical, shopping)?
- Do we want beach, jungle, or “green views”?
- What’s our rainy-day routine plan?
- Who is our community (people we’ll see weekly)?

## A quiet-life plan that works

The quietest families tend to do two things well:

1) **Build a weekly rhythm** (market day, activity day, “big errands” day)  
2) **Stay connected** (a consistent class, group, or community touchpoint)

## Next steps

- Compare areas quickly: [/areas](/areas)
- Plan a test stay: [/guides/two-week-test-stay-plan](/guides/two-week-test-stay-plan)
- If you’re balancing budget too: [/costs](/costs)

guides.title: Renting safely in Bali (questions to ask before deposits)
guides.description: A parent-first renting guide: verification steps, contract questions, and a staged approach that reduces risk.
guides.body:
## Quick take

Safe renting is mostly about slowing the process down enough that identity, money, and expectations can all be verified before pressure takes over.

## The non-negotiables

### Verify who you are dealing with
Know who is representing the property and how that relationship is established.

### Verify how payment works
Get clarity on what is due, when, to whom, and under what written conditions.

### Verify what the agreement actually includes
Furniture, utilities, maintenance, internet, staff, cleaning, repairs, notice, and deposit terms should not live only in chat messages.

## Family-specific watchouts

- a house that is beautiful but creates a punishing week,
- poor communication around maintenance,
- vague deposit language,
- pressure to commit before you have tested the area honestly.

## A safer family sequence

1. Shortlist the area.  
2. Build the brief.  
3. View or verify.  
4. Read the terms slowly.  
5. Only then move money.

## Best companion pages

- [Housing intro readiness](/housing-intro-readiness)
- [Housing brief builder](/housing-brief-builder)
- [Lease and deposit questions](/guides/lease-and-deposit-questions-in-bali)

guides.title: The 2‑week test-stay plan (before you commit to Bali)
guides.description: A practical test-stay plan for families—how to choose 2–3 areas, simulate routines, and avoid “holiday mode” decisions.

faqs.q: Is two weeks enough to decide?
faqs.a: Two weeks is often enough to learn what daily life feels like (school run, errands, evenings). Many families still do a longer second trip before signing a lease.

faqs.q: How many areas should we try in one visit?
faqs.a: Usually 2–3 areas. More than that turns into constant packing and moving, and you never get a routine.

faqs.q: What should we avoid during a test stay?
faqs.a: Avoid signing long contracts, making school decisions on day one, and booking an accommodation that is too “vacation-perfect” to represent daily life.

guides.body:
## Quick start
- Pick **2–3 areas** using this: [Area shortlist scorecard](/resources/area-shortlist-scorecard)
- For each area, schedule:
  - one “work morning”
  - one “errands afternoon”
  - one “quiet evening”
- Do at least **one rainy day plan** (even if it’s dry season)

Related: [Bali areas for families](/areas) · [Where to live in Bali (guide)](/guides/where-to-live-in-bali-for-families)

## Step 1: Decide what “good” means for your family
Write down your top 3:
- calm mornings
- walkable errands
- community
- green space
- kid activities
- commute simplicity
- budget control

Then pick your “non-negotiable”:
- *We can’t do daily heavy traffic*, or
- *We need walkable basics*, or
- *We need quiet sleep.*

## Step 2: Choose 2–3 areas (not 6)
Shortlists that work:
- **Ubud + Sanur** (nature + calmer beach city)
- **Canggu region + Sanur** (international energy + calmer backup)
- **Ubud + Canggu region** (two very different lifestyles)

Comparison guide: [Ubud vs Sanur vs Canggu for families](/guides/ubud-vs-sanur-vs-canggu-for-families)

## Step 3: Book accommodation that matches real life
A test stay is not a honeymoon. We recommend:
- a place with a kitchen (or easy food options nearby)
- a location that allows you to do “school run timing”
- reliable internet (if you’re working)

Guide: [Phones and internet in Bali](/guides/phones-and-internet-in-bali)

## Step 4: Run “routine simulations”

### Optional: add a kids “anchor” (camp or weekly program)

If you’re doing a test stay, one simple way to avoid “holiday mode” is to give kids a predictable anchor for a few days:
- a short holiday camp, or
- a weekly program that runs during the week.

It’s not required—but for many families it makes the visit more realistic (kids have structure, parents can do errands and calls).

Start here:
- [Camps & short-term programs](/camps)
- [Camp questions checklist (copy/paste)](/resources/camp-questions-checklist)

### Simulation A: morning routine
- breakfast
- school/run timing (even if you aren’t enrolled)
- commute test (10–20 minutes driving)

### Simulation B: errands + groceries
- grocery shop
- pharmacy
- quick meal plan
- see how long it takes and how it feels

Guide: [Groceries and routines in Bali](/guides/groceries-meals-routines-in-bali)

### Simulation C: evening + sleep
- dinner
- bedtime
- noise check
- mosquito plan check

Safety guide: [Safety basics for families](/guides/bali-safety-basics-for-families)

## Step 5: Write your notes the same day
Use three prompts:
1. What felt easy today?
2. What felt stressful today?
3. If we did this for 6 months, what would break?

## What we learned the hard way
Families often decide from a “perfect day.” The best decisions come from an ordinary day.

## Next steps
- If you haven’t, read: [Start here](/start-here)
- If you’re getting serious about housing: [Renting safely in Bali](/guides/renting-safely-in-bali)
- If you’re comparing neighborhoods: [Bali area guides](/areas)

guides.title: Ubud vs Sanur vs Canggu for families (how to choose)
guides.description: A calm comparison: pace, routines, community, commute, and “what it feels like” day-to-day—so you can shortlist areas without overthinking.

faqs.q: Which area is best for families?
faqs.a: There isn’t one best. It depends on your family’s pace, commute tolerance, and what you want daily life to feel like.

faqs.q: Is Canggu too busy for kids?
faqs.a: Some families love the energy and community; others find it overstimulating. A short test stay is the easiest way to know.

faqs.q: Is Ubud better for calmer routines?
faqs.a: Many families find it calmer and greener, but it depends on your exact location and your daily needs (activities, services, community).

guides.body:
## Quick comparison (the vibe)
- **Ubud:** green, slower, more “inward,” great for families who want calmer routines
- **Sanur:** beach city energy, easier errands, often a calmer “base”
- **Canggu region:** international, busy, lots happening, more traffic and stimulation

If you haven’t yet, start here: [Area guides](/areas)

## How to decide (the only 3 questions that matter)
### 1) What pace makes your family calm?
- Do you love “always something on”?
- Or do you want quiet evenings and nature?

### 2) What commute stress can you tolerate?
Some families are fine with driving. Others find it drains energy fast.

### 3) What does “community” mean for you?
- international community and events?
- quieter neighbor friendships?
- school community as your main anchor?

## Ubud (family notes)
Good fit if:
- you want green space and calmer routines
- you like slower mornings
Watch-outs:
- some locations feel isolated without a good transport plan

Area guide: [Ubud for families](/areas/ubud)

## Sanur (family notes)
Good fit if:
- you want an easier “base”
- you like walkable errands and a more established vibe
Area guide: [Sanur for families](/areas/sanur)

## Canggu region (family notes)
Good fit if:
- you want a lot happening and a big community
- you like activities and cafes
Watch-outs:
- traffic and stimulation can be real

Area guides:
- [Canggu](/areas/canggu)
- [Berawa](/areas/berawa)
- [Pererenan](/areas/pererenan)

## What we learned the hard way
Families often fall in love with an area on a perfect day. Try to include at least one ordinary day: errands, tired kids, and bedtime.

## Next steps
- [2‑week test stay plan](/guides/two-week-test-stay-plan)
- [Renting safely in Bali](/guides/renting-safely-in-bali)
- [Start here](/start-here)

guides.title: Visa scam red flags (and how families protect themselves)
guides.description: Anonymous, practical red flags that help families avoid scams without naming or accusing specific people.

faqs.q: What if an agent says “guaranteed approval”?
faqs.a: Treat it as a red flag. Rules change and outcomes depend on circumstances. Look for an agent who speaks in probabilities and verification.

guides.body:
## Quick take

A scam usually becomes visible through pressure, vagueness, or unrealistic confidence long before it becomes visible through one dramatic detail.

## Red flags that deserve extra caution

### Urgency without a paper trail
If the message is basically “pay quickly or lose the chance,” slow down.

### Big promises with fuzzy language
Anything that sounds too certain about approvals, timing, or “special access” deserves more scrutiny.

### Weak business identity
If it is hard to understand who the provider is, how they work, or what service they are actually charging for, treat that as meaningful information.

### Payment pressure that outruns clarity
Important payments should follow a clear explanation of service, timing, and responsibility.

## Family rule of thumb

When a visa process starts sounding like a secret shortcut, your safest move is usually to step back and verify through official sources and calmer channels.

## Use this page well

- Confirm the visa lane first.
- Keep screenshots and documents organised.
- Be extra cautious when anything changes quickly.
- Use official links to verify the parts that can move.

## Related

- [Visas](/visas)
- [Official links](/official-links)
- [How to choose a visa agent](/guides/how-to-choose-a-visa-agent)

guides.title: What to ask on a school tour (copy/paste checklist)
guides.description: A copy/paste list of questions for school tours—learning support, safety, communication, community, and commute reality.
guides.body:
## Quick take

A good school tour is not mainly for collecting answers. It is for noticing whether the day around Empathy School feels more possible or less.

## The five things parents should actually look for

### 1. Emotional temperature
Does the campus feel settled, rushed, performative, or genuinely lived in?

### 2. Adult presence
Do adults feel relational and observant, especially in transitions — not just polished during the formal talking points?

### 3. Child fit
Would your child soften here, resist here, need more time here, or need something fundamentally different?

### 4. Transition support
How are arrival, movement between spaces, and the wobblier moments of the day handled?

### 5. Weekly effect
What would this school do to your mornings, area choice, pickup energy, and after-school rhythm?

## Questions worth asking

- What tends to help children settle well here?
- What usually makes the first weeks harder?
- How do families use a tour or a test stay to judge fit realistically?
- What should we notice about the commute, not just the campus?

## Best practice after the tour

Leave with notes on three things only:

- what felt like a strong fit,
- what still feels unclear,
- what the school would change about where and how you live in Bali.

## Pair this with

- [Empathy School fit](/empathy-school-fit)
- [Empathy School tour prep](/empathy-school-tour-prep)
- [School tour question list](/resources/school-tour-question-list)

guides.title: Where to live in Bali for families: how to shortlist areas
guides.description: A calm approach to choosing where to live: pace, noise, walkability, commute, and your family’s real priorities.
guides.body:
## Quick take

The best Bali area for a family is rarely the most famous one. It is the one that still feels workable on a tired weekday.

## Start with the real filters

### Your child’s regulation needs
Do they need a calmer radius, easier movement, and fewer inputs — or do they warm up through activity and variety?

### Your adult bandwidth
A beautiful base is not automatically right if it creates more driving, more decisions, and less buffer for the adults.

### Whether Empathy School matters
If Empathy School is a real part of the move, it should influence area choice early rather than becoming a commute surprise later.

### Your move shape
A test stay, a 3-month season, and a longer relocation do not need the same kind of base.

## A practical shortlist method

1. Pick **one calmer option**.
2. Pick **one more convenient option**.
3. If needed, pick **one values-first option** that reflects what you hope Bali will feel like.
4. Compare those three through commute, food loop, child energy, and how the adults feel by evening.

## Common area mistakes

- choosing by villa photos instead of family radius,
- assuming “close enough” drives will still feel fine after week three,
- picking an area adults enjoy online more than children enjoy in real life.

guides.title: Your first week in Bali: setup checklist for families
guides.description: A practical first-week checklist: SIM, transport, routines, groceries, healthcare plan, and what to postpone.
guides.body:
## Quick take

The first week does not need to be impressive. It needs to become **repeatable** fast enough that the family stops solving every basic thing from scratch.

## The first-week priorities

1. **Transport you understand**  
   Decide how you will do the next three school-like mornings before you do anything optional.

2. **A food loop that works when everyone is tired**  
   Find one grocery route, one breakfast default, one easy lunch, and one fallback dinner that does not create more thinking.

3. **Phone + internet stability**  
   Get your connection sorted early so maps, messages, work calls, and delivery apps are not fragile.

4. **One child anchor**  
   Even a tiny anchor matters: a tour, a camp day, the same park, the same café stop, the same evening ritual.

5. **A paper trail**  
   Keep photos or files for passports, entry documents, school notes, housing messages, and payment receipts in one place.

## A simple first-week sequence

### Day 1–2
- Land, rest, and keep the radius very small.
- Confirm transport basics.
- Set up water, snacks, and easy meals.
- Do not schedule the hardest decision on the first tired day.

### Day 3–4
- Run one ordinary morning.
- Pressure-test the commute or area route you are most likely to repeat.
- Buy the small things that make evenings calmer: chargers, rain cover, simple medicines, extra water bottles.

### Day 5–7
- Decide what is still unclear: area, school, housing, or budget.
- Use the rest of the stay or month to answer that question on purpose.
- Keep the family schedule lighter than your research brain wants.

## What families regret most

- trying to solve housing, school, visas, and community in the same forty-eight hours,  
- moving around too much,  
- letting adults stay in planning mode while children are already in adaptation mode.

## Best companion pages

- [First Month Planner](/first-month-planner)
- [Weekday Reality](/weekday-reality)
- [Daily Life](/daily-life)

blog.title: A 10-day test stay: what a composite family learned
blog.description: A composite family story about how one short Bali stay created better decisions through ordinary days, not a packed itinerary.

faqs.q: Can a 10-day stay tell us anything useful?
faqs.a: Yes — if you protect ordinary time. A shorter stay can still create signal around area fit, school interest, daily rhythm, and what parts of the move still feel vague.

faqs.q: Should we pack a test stay with activities?
faqs.a: Usually no. Families often learn more from one grocery run, one school day, and one tired evening than from filling the stay with outings.

faqs.q: What is the best question to leave a test stay with?
faqs.a: A specific next-step question: which area deserves a second look, whether Empathy School should stay in the plan, or whether the move should stay staged longer.

blog.body:
## First, the honesty note

This is a **composite family story**.

It is not a direct testimonial from one named family.
It is a realistic pattern built from the kinds of questions families ask when they start using Bali as a real decision rather than a dream.

## The setup

Picture two parents working remotely, with children aged 5 and 8.

They are excited, but cautious.
They have already done too much online research.
They have too many tabs open, too many areas saved, and too many opinions in their head at the same time.

So they decide on a 10-day stay.
Not a holiday.
A test.

Their goals are simple:
- feel two realistic areas,
- see whether Empathy School belongs in the next round of planning,
- test weekday energy,
- learn whether the adults still like the idea by the middle of the week.

## What they expected to matter

Before arriving, they thought the biggest signal would come from:
- villa viewings,
- neighborhood vibe,
- whether the children said “I love it here,”
- and whether Bali felt exciting enough.

That turned out to be the wrong list.

## What actually mattered

The biggest signal came from smaller, quieter moments.

### 1. One ordinary morning

They left enough space for a slower morning.
Breakfast.
A short drive.
A school-related visit.
Some waiting.
A child who was a little tired.
An adult who still needed to answer work messages.

That single morning did more than the glossy parts of the trip.
It showed them what the move might feel like once nobody was trying to perform enjoyment.

### 2. One school-adjacent day

The family had been unsure whether school should shape the move early.
A visit around Empathy School changed that.

Not because they instantly decided yes.
Because they suddenly had a better question:

**Would we like our week around this school?**

That is a much better question than “Did we like the visit?”

### 3. One tired evening

The most useful part of the trip was not a highlight.
It was a slightly flat evening.
A longer-than-ideal drive.
Hungry children.
Adults who were not at their best.

That moment made the family realize something important:

They did not need the “best” Bali version.
They needed the version that still felt kind on a hard day.

## What changed after the trip

They did **not** leave with every answer.
That is not what a good test stay does.

They left with a smaller, stronger decision set:
- one area dropped off the list,
- one area deserved a second look,
- Empathy School moved from “maybe later” to “worth testing properly,”
- and the move stayed staged rather than becoming rushed.

That is a successful short stay.

## The real lesson

A useful test stay is not about getting a perfect yes.

It is about reducing noise.

The family learned that Bali only became clearer when they stopped trying to prove the move and started noticing the ordinary week.

## If you want to copy the useful part

Protect these things in your own test stay:
- one normal weekday,
- one school-related moment if school matters,
- one area comparison that includes real travel,
- one tired-time observation,
- one written decision at the end.

blog.body:
## This is a composite story

This is not a verbatim testimonial.
It is a composite family scenario built from a very common pattern:
parents like two areas online, then one school run changes the whole conversation.

## The setup

The family has narrowed things down to two areas.
On screen, both still look good.

Area one feels more exciting.
Area two feels calmer.

Before arrival, the adults keep talking like this is still a taste question.
Which area feels more “us”?
Which one looks nicer?
Which one seems more alive?

Then they test a real route connected to Empathy School.

## What happened

The route did not go badly.
That was not the issue.

It simply revealed more than expected.

The family noticed:
- how the morning pace changed,
- how much margin they still had after the drive,
- whether the adults felt depleted or okay,
- what pickup energy might feel like later in the day,
- and whether the area still looked attractive once transport became part of daily life.

The result was not dramatic.
It was clearer than that.

One area still worked.
The other area suddenly felt heavier.

## Why this changed the shortlist

Because the family stopped choosing an area as a mood.
They started choosing an area as a **week**.

That is the move.
Not the café list.
Not the online hype.
Not the idea of who lives there.

The week.

## What the family learned

### 1. Commute is not a side detail

It shapes:
- adult patience,
- child energy,
- after-school rhythm,
- how often you say yes to one more outing,
- and whether the family still likes the move on a tired day.

### 2. School fit and area fit are connected

The school decision is never only the school decision.
If Empathy School matters, it changes the housing and area conversation too.

### 3. The calmer option may win later than it wins online

The quieter, less exciting area often becomes more attractive once the family imagines the third week, not the first weekend.

## The lesson to copy

If Empathy School is in the picture, do not choose an area without at least one realistic school-run test.

The route does not need to be perfect.
It only needs to tell the truth.

blog.body:
## Written answer first

Early Years fit is often decided by things that are easy to miss in a normal tour.

Parents of younger children are usually trying to answer quieter questions:

- would my child feel held here,
- would mornings feel safer or more strained,
- and does the emotional temperature of the space match what my child needs.

That is what this video is good for.

---

## What to watch for

### 1) Emotional temperature

Does the space feel warm enough for small children?

Not just attractive.
Warm.
Held.
Regulated.

### 2) Transition support

Young children live inside transitions.
Arrival, snack, movement, toileting, shifting attention.

If those moments look thoughtful, it is a good sign.
If they look rushed, parents usually feel it quickly.

### 3) Scale and sensory load

A younger child may love a nature-rich environment and still get tired by the overall stimulation.

Watch for:
- visual busyness,
- sound,
- movement,
- and whether the space feels expansive in a soothing way or a draining way.

### 4) Your own body response

This is more useful than it sounds.

After watching, do you feel your shoulders drop a little?
Or do you still feel a low-level “I’m not sure.”

That signal matters.

---

## What this recap is really for

This video is not asking you to decide admissions from a screen.

It is helping you decide whether an in-person visit is worth structuring your week around, and whether Empathy School belongs in the move conversation early.

## Written answer first

Middle school decisions are rarely only about academics or campus feel.

They are also about dignity, social fit, independence, and whether the broader Bali lifestyle works for an older child.

That is why this recap matters.
It helps parents watch for whether the environment feels genuinely age-appropriate.

---

## What to watch for

### 1) Dignity

Older children usually know quickly when a space feels too young, too performative, or not designed with them in mind.

Watch the tone of the environment, not just the rooms.

### 2) Voice

Does the culture look like one where older children can be thoughtful and visible?
Or does it feel like they are simply expected to fit an existing mould?

### 3) Belonging

For this age, belonging matters almost as much as learning.

A video cannot answer social fit in full.
But it can tell you whether the environment feels flat, pressured, or alive.

### 4) Bigger lifestyle fit

If your child is older, the school decision touches the whole move:
- the pace of life,
- social options,
- commute tolerance,
- how much quiet or stimulation feels right.

---

## A better next step

If this video makes Empathy School feel plausible, widen the question just a little.

Do not ask only, “Would this school work?”
Ask, “Would this school plus this version of Bali work for this stage of our family life?”

### 3) Outdoor rhythm

Empathy School’s environment matters.
But what matters more is how the outdoor energy feels in relation to your child.

For some families, this is the reason the school feels obvious.
For others, it reveals that they still need more time or a different pace.

### 4) Weekly effect

A school does not sit in isolation.

If this school feels likely, it changes:
- your housing radius,
- your commute tolerance,
- your pickup energy,
- and sometimes the entire emotional shape of the move.

That is why this video belongs in a relocation hub, not only on a school page.

---

## What to watch in the first minute

If you only have a short window, pay attention to:

- whether the space feels calm or merely quiet,
- whether adults seem relational,
- whether you can imagine your child here on a completely normal day,
- whether your body says “this could work” or “I still can’t picture it.”

That last answer matters more than any polished talking point.

---

## What this video cannot answer for you

A tour video can help.
It cannot decide for you.

It will not tell you:
- how your child will feel after three weeks,
- what the school run does to the week,
- whether Ubud-side living genuinely suits your family,
- or whether your adult bandwidth is strong enough for this version of the move.

If the video makes Empathy School feel more likely, do not keep watching more clips without a plan.

Instead:
1. decide whether school fit should enter the move now,
2. protect enough time around the tour day,
3. use the school to test the week, not just the campus.
