blog.title: What a rainy week taught one family about routine
blog.description: A composite family story about how one rainy week made a Bali move feel more real — and more workable.

faqs.q: Why does rainy season matter so much in family planning?
faqs.a: Because it tests your defaults. A family rhythm that only works in ideal weather may feel fragile very quickly once transport, indoor time, and tired afternoons change.

faqs.q: What helps most during rainy stretches in Bali with kids?
faqs.a: Simpler plans, indoor backups, calmer after-school expectations, and fewer moving parts in the week.

faqs.q: Should we wait to think about daily life until after we move?
faqs.a: No. Daily-life planning is one of the fastest ways to see whether a move plan feels sustainable or only exciting.

blog.body:
## This is a composite story

This story is built from a recurring pattern, not a single published testimonial.

Families often feel surprisingly clear about Bali after one rainy week — not because rain is bad, but because it reveals whether the move has good defaults.

## The setup

The family has done many things right.
They have a good housing base.
They have a rough routine.
They feel positive.

Then the weather turns.

Nothing dramatic.
Just several days where rain keeps changing the plan.

## What the week exposed

The family starts to notice where their Bali plan is strong and where it is still too dependent on ideal conditions.

Rain changes:
- pickup timing,
- how long simple drives feel,
- how much outdoor movement the children get,
- adult patience,
- and how much improvisation the week can tolerate.

By the second or third wet day, the family realizes something useful.

They do not need a more ambitious rhythm.
They need a better **default rhythm**.

## What improved things fastest

### 1. Fewer afternoon expectations

They stop trying to rescue each day.
Afternoons get simpler.
The whole house gets calmer.

### 2. One reliable indoor backup

Not ten ideas.
One or two defaults the family can use without discussion.

### 3. More honest energy accounting

They begin planning the week around how everyone actually feels by late afternoon.
That changes everything.

## Why this matters for the move

Because daily life is where the move either becomes sustainable or fragile.

Families often think the big decisions are:
- visa,
- housing,
- school,
- budget.

Those matter.

But a move can still feel hard if the ordinary week has no calm defaults.
Rain simply reveals that sooner.

## The lesson

Do not wait for stress to teach you your family defaults.
Build them before you need them.

blog.body:
## The honesty note

This is a **composite family story**.
It is based on a pattern that shows up again and again when families begin looking at rentals before their move shape is clear enough.

## The setup

A family has arrived at the housing stage too fast.
They have favorite villas saved.
The photos are beautiful.
The interiors feel calm.
The price looks good enough to stay emotionally attached.

They are asking the wrong early question:

**Which house do we like most?**

The better question would have been:

**Which house makes our actual week lighter?**

## What changed the story

Once they start testing the week more honestly, the photos lose power.

They begin asking:
- How far is this from the routes that matter?
- What happens when a child is tired?
- What does pickup feel like from here?
- What kind of maintenance load does this home create?
- What is included and what is not?
- Would we still like this home after rain, traffic, and errands become normal?

That is when the shortlist changes.

## The surprise

The prettiest property is no longer the most convincing one.

A simpler option begins to look stronger because:
- it reduces daily driving,
- it makes the week more forgiving,
- it creates fewer maintenance unknowns,
- and it gives the adults a little more end-of-day margin.

That margin matters.

## Where Gaia Group fits

This is exactly why the housing lane in the hub stays narrow.
The point is not to create more listings.
It is to make the housing conversation more specific.

A good intro to Gaia Group works best when the family already knows:
- likely move timing,
- approximate budget band,
- two or three realistic areas,
- must-haves,
- and dealbreakers.

That is how housing stops being a mood board and starts becoming a useful brief.

## The lesson

Housing is a systems decision.

Rent, drive time, school, groceries, tired children, rainy days, and maintenance all touch each other.

If the house only works when everyone is fresh and the roads are kind, it may not be the right house.

blog.title: The 45,000‑Rupiah Miracle
blog.description: How Bali quietly makes family life feel easy
blog.body:
By Eric

Some mornings in Bali start with a soundtrack you didn’t know you needed.

A rooster somewhere in the distance. The soft clink of temple bells. A scooter humming past slowly—less “rush hour,” more “someone’s going to buy fruit.” Incense drifting in from a tiny offering placed neatly on the edge of a driveway. My kids outside, barefoot, already inventing a game out of sticks and leaves and whatever the jungle decides to contribute that day.

It’s the kind of scene people fly across the world to witness for a week.

And yet the thing that still surprises me most isn’t the beauty. It’s the convenience.

Because in the background of all that calm—rice fields flowing like green water, the jungle breathing, the space to actually hear yourself think—Bali has quietly built something that makes daily family life feel… manageable. Even comfortable. Sometimes weirdly effortless.

The number that captures it best is 45,000 rupiah.

That’s the delivery fee I pay for groceries when I don’t want to turn the day into a traffic mission. Less than $3 for someone to bring what my family needs right to our door.

It sounds like a small detail. It’s not.

The best Bali days don’t begin in a car

When families imagine moving to Bali, they picture the big things first:

Nature

Community

A slower pace

A healthier rhythm for their kids

All true.

But the part you only learn by living here is that your day-to-day happiness often depends on the small things: How easy is it to get what you need? How often do errands hijack your schedule? How much time do you spend stuck in transit instead of actually living?

That’s where Bali has been a joyful surprise for me.

If I need something—anything from household essentials to random “we ran out of that and my kids will absolutely notice” items—I open Tokopedia or Shopee, search, tap, and it’s handled. What still amazes me is how often it’s more affordable than America, and how reliably it just works.

It’s not flashy. It’s just… supportive.

And for a family, support is everything.

“Western groceries” without the weekly expedition

I still like going to big grocery stores sometimes. There’s something satisfying about it—choosing, browsing, finding a new snack you didn’t know existed.

But I don’t want that to be my default rhythm. I don’t want “getting groceries” to be a project that consumes half a day and all my patience.

So for many of our staples—especially the “Western products” my family likes—I use online grocery services like Delta online.

And then that number shows up again:

Rp 45,000.

Not just a fee—more like a quiet life upgrade.

Because what that buys isn’t only delivery. It buys time. It buys energy. It buys the kind of afternoon where you’re not recovering from errands—you’re actually present for your kids.

Fresh vegetables that don’t require a plan

Then there’s the produce side of life, where Bali shines in its own way.

For vegetables, I use Bali Jiva.

There’s something deeply satisfying about waking up in a place with temples and rice fields and sunlight pouring in—then having crisp greens show up without you needing to navigate the day around it.

It’s one of those “pinch me” moments: you can live near nature without feeling cut off from the modern world.

(The main idea is the system: let delivery handle errands so your days stay calm.)

Ubud: incredible… and optional

Ubud is special. There are truly great restaurants there. The kind of place you go for a meal that feels like a celebration—without needing a special occasion.

But here’s the honest part: the traffic can be intense.

And what I’ve learned is that you don’t have to build your life around the busiest places to enjoy them. You can treat Ubud like a destination you visit when you want that experience—then come back to the version of Bali that feels like it was designed for families.

For us, that’s the area in and around Empathy School.

This is the Bali I didn’t just want to visit. This is the Bali I wanted my kids to grow inside of:

Flowing rice fields that change color with the season

Jungle edges that feel alive, not manicured

Space—real space—for kids to play

A sense of safety and peace that settles into your body

When you live somewhere like this, convenience isn’t about luxury. It’s about preserving the calm you came here for.

The real “Bali hack” for families

People sometimes ask what makes day-to-day life work here as a parent.

My answer is simple: don’t fight the island. Let it carry you.

Here’s what that looks like in our life:

Use Tokopedia + Shopee when you need “stuff” quickly and easily.

Use Delta online when you want groceries without a long outing.

Use Bali Jiva to keep vegetables fresh and effortless.

Go to Ubud for the magic—without making it your weekly commute.

Build your everyday life around nature, space, and calm—then let delivery handle the logistics.

This is how you get the best of both worlds: the Bali people dream about, plus the Bali that actually functions when you have kids and routines and real-life needs.

Why this feels so good

There’s a particular kind of joy that happens when you move somewhere beautiful and realize you don’t have to sacrifice practicality to enjoy it.

It’s not just that the kids are happier (though they are). It’s not just that the surroundings are stunning (they are).

It’s that your days stop being dominated by “life admin.”

Instead of spending your best hours in traffic, you spend them listening to the temple sounds drift through the morning. Watching your kids build something imaginative out of nothing. Walking near rice fields that look like they’ve been painted fresh overnight.

And somewhere in the middle of all that, a delivery arrives.

Groceries. Vegetables. The little things.

Handled.

That’s the 45,000‑rupiah miracle.

blog.title: Why I Feel So Safe Raising Kids in Bali
blog.description: When families talk to me about moving to Bali, “Is it safe?” is usually the first real question.
blog.body:
When families talk to me about moving to Bali, “Is it safe?” is usually the first real question.

I understand it. Safety isn’t a headline. It’s a daily feeling. It’s whether you can relax while your kids grow up. It’s whether ordinary life stays ordinary.

So instead of trying to convince you with big statements, I’ll just share what safety looks like in our family’s day-to-day life here—simple routines, small rules, and a community that makes it easy to exhale.

The Best Safety Upgrade We Made Was… Geography

Our house is near Empathy School.

That one detail changes everything.

It means my kids can walk to school. It means mornings don’t start with traffic and rushing and stress. It means the school isn’t a distant destination—it’s part of the neighborhood.

Most mornings, my two boys walk together. Sometimes I’m with them. Sometimes their mom is with them. Sometimes it’s just the two of them, heading down the lane with their backpacks and their own little conversations.

It’s one of those scenes that still makes me smile every time. It’s calm. It’s sweet. And for me, it’s a huge part of why Bali feels so safe: the place is built for real life, not constant guarding and managing.

The 6:00 PM Rule That Makes Everyone’s Life Easier

My older son is 12, which is the age where independence starts to arrive in steady waves.

He’ll often tell me he’s going to a friend’s house. My rule is straightforward:

You can go.

Tell me in advance.

Be home by 6:00 PM.

Sometimes he forgets to tell me ahead of time. He’s 12. It happens. But most of the time, he remembers.

And the 6:00 PM boundary works for a few practical reasons: the daylight fades quickly, it’s dinner time, and I don’t want another family to feel like they’re responsible for feeding my kid every night.

What I love most is how little “management” this requires. I don’t need a long explanation of where he’ll be every minute. I don’t need a detailed plan. He’s with friends. Sometimes he brings friends to our house, sometimes he’s at theirs.

It’s easy. It feels normal.

That’s the kind of safety parents are really looking for.

A Road That’s Not Built for Speed Helps More Than You’d Think

There’s a small detail between our home and the school that makes a big difference: the road isn’t especially friendly to fast cars.

It naturally slows things down. It’s more human-scale. That’s a big deal when you have kids walking around.

In many places, a parent’s worry is shaped by traffic more than anything else. Here, the environment itself encourages slower movement and more awareness. For walking children, that matters every single day.

The Dogs Are Part of the Neighborhood

Yes, there are dogs around. That’s common in Bali.

In our area, they’re not strangers. My kids know the dogs. I know the dogs. They feel like part of the neighborhood, not a threat.

There are also periodic vaccination drives in the community, which helps everyone feel more comfortable. And if something ever feels off, there’s usually a direct, human solution: talk to the neighbor who looks after that dog.

One of the most comforting things about Bali is that people are receptive. If you bring a concern respectfully, you’re usually met with respect in return.

Community Is a Kind of Security System

The Balinese community around us is warm and open. We get invited to temples and ceremonies and shared experiences. There’s a feeling of being included, not kept at arm’s length.

And that’s not just “nice.” It’s protective.

When you know your neighbors—and they know you—kids are more visible. People notice. People help. It’s not formal. It’s just how daily life works.

Safety is often created by relationship.

A Quick Story About the Police: Calm, Capable, and Close By

A while back, we donated money to help the local police build a radio tower so they could communicate more easily with one another. The school also has a channel on that network.

We’ve never needed to use it. But it’s there.

That matters to me—not because I expect emergencies, but because it’s reassuring to know the local systems are real and reachable.

When I visited the police station, I asked—mostly out of curiosity—if I could see the jail area. They showed me, and it was… dusty. Cobwebs and all.

I asked when they last used it.

Their answer was almost charming: the last “situation” was a very drunk farmer they couldn’t get home safely, so they let him sleep there for the night.

That was it.

Not dramatic. Not scary. Just a community handling a small human problem in a practical way.

Even the School Has Been Treated With Respect

One of the things I’m most grateful for is this: over the years, we haven’t experienced vandalism on campus. We haven’t had people breaking in and damaging the school.

That doesn’t mean nothing ever happens anywhere. It just reflects what we’ve lived: a strong baseline of respect for shared spaces, for children, and for the community.

What Safety Looks Like for Us, in Simple Terms

If I had to summarize the habits and conditions that make Bali feel so safe for our family, it would be these:

We live close enough to walk, so kids aren’t dependent on cars and long commutes.

We keep rules simple, like “tell us first” and “home by 6.”

The neighborhood moves at a slower pace, especially on the smaller roads.

There’s a sense of community presence, not isolation.

Local support is accessible, and people are responsive when you talk to them.

And maybe most importantly: the feeling of safety here isn’t something I have to work hard to create. It’s something the environment supports.

If You’re Considering Bali

If you’re thinking about moving your family here, I won’t tell you to ignore your questions. Ask them. Visit. Walk around the neighborhoods you might live in. Notice how your body feels during an ordinary morning.

In our life here—raising a 12-year-old and a five-year-old—Bali has felt peaceful, welcoming, and deeply safe.

And I don’t take that for granted.

—Eric (Founder, Empathy School)

blog.title: Rainy season with kids: what changes (and what doesn’t)

blog.body:
## The mistake is treating rain like an interruption

Families usually get calmer when they stop seeing rain as the day going wrong and start treating it like a design constraint.

## What rainy weeks are really testing

Rain exposes whether you have:

- an indoor backup,
- a food plan,
- a calmer after-school routine,
- and enough margin that one soggy afternoon does not collapse the whole mood.

## What tends to help

- two or three indoor defaults the children already know,
- less ambitious afternoon planning,
- spare clothes and shoes where you actually need them,
- a lower bar for what counts as a successful day.

## The bigger move lesson

Rainy season is not only about weather. It is about whether the family week is sturdy enough to absorb inconvenience without becoming emotional chaos.

## The calm decision is rarely the fastest one

A calm move is not passive. It is deliberate.

Families usually feel calmer when they stop demanding one giant yes-or-no answer and start building the move in smaller truths:

- we know our likely timeline,
- we know our two or three areas,
- we know whether Empathy School should change the move,
- we know what kind of week we are actually trying to create.

## What “calm” usually looks like in practice

It often means:

- a staged move instead of one dramatic leap,
- fewer irreversible decisions early,
- a smaller area shortlist,
- and enough honesty to notice when a beautiful plan would be too heavy in real life.

## The question that helps most

Instead of asking “Should we move to Bali?” try asking:

**What would make Bali feel sustainable for our family by week three, not just day three?**

That question usually produces better action than more inspiration.

blog.title: 3 budgeting mistakes families make when planning Bali
blog.description: A few common mistakes—and a calmer way to plan ranges instead of one fragile number.
blog.body:
## Mistake #1: Treating Bali like one number

A single number sounds neat, but it hides the real question: **which version of the week are you pricing?**

A Bali budget changes a lot once area, transport, and whether Empathy School shapes the move become real.

## Mistake #2: Looking at rent before looking at radius

A lower rent can still create a heavier month if it means:

- longer drives,
- more driver use,
- more meals out because the day runs late,
- and less tolerance for the home by the middle of the week.

## Mistake #3: Underestimating setup month

The first month often includes:

- deposits,
- short stays,
- transport experiments,
- extra purchases,
- and the cost of not yet knowing your easy defaults.

## Mistake #4: Forgetting that learning changes the whole plan

On this hub, the school question means Empathy School, tours, camps, or a school-shaped week. Once learning enters the move, budget assumptions often change quickly.

## A calmer approach

Build a **low / mid / high** range, then test it against two realistic areas and one likely housing style.

faqs.q: Why does this planner matter so much?

faqs.q: What should we decide first?

faqs.q: Can we use this on a test stay?

resources.body:
## Fill this in before the week begins

- Who handles pickup?
- Is the route home direct?
- What one extra stop are we **not** doing?

### Food plan
- What snack is waiting?
- What is the easiest dinner if the child is already tired?
- What adult task can wait until after food?

- Does this child usually need quiet, movement, connection, or alone time first?
- What will make that easier today?

### Evening plan
- What time do we want the house to start getting softer?
- What needs to be ready for tomorrow?
- What can be skipped if everyone is done?

resources.title: Empathy School commute decision grid
resources.description: A practical decision grid for testing whether an area still works once the Empathy School route becomes part of the family week.
resources.body:
## Use this when

Empathy School is moving from abstract idea to real decision.

This grid helps you judge whether an area still works once the school route becomes part of:
- mornings,
- pickups,
- adult work windows,
- and how much family energy is left by late afternoon.

## Score each area from 1–5

### Morning calm
How likely is this area to protect a steady school morning?

### Route predictability
Does the route feel repeatable or fragile?

### After-school energy
Would the child and adults still have margin after the return?

### Adult work protection
Can work still happen without the route dominating the whole day?

### Housing compatibility
Does the housing radius still make sense if Empathy School matters more?

### Long-term honesty
Does the area still feel like a good idea once you imagine repeating this route for real?

## Questions to write under the score

- What part of the school route feels easiest here?
- What part of the school route feels most fragile?
- If we chose this area, what would housing need to optimize for?
- Are we keeping the area because it truly works, or because we like the story of it?

## Best use of the result

A lower score does not automatically eliminate an area.
It tells you what the area is costing.

Then you can decide whether that cost is worth paying.

## Related

- [Commute reality](/commute-reality)
- [Compare areas](/compare-areas)
- [Empathy School](/schools)

resources.title: Empathy School tour day plan
resources.description: A calmer sample schedule for families who want an Empathy School visit to reveal something real about the move.
resources.body:
## Use this as a sample day, not a rigid script

The point is to keep enough space around the visit that the day still feels real.

## Sample plan

### Night before

- confirm the start time,
- keep dinner and bedtime simple,
- charge phones,
- prepare a notes app or paper sheet,
- pack water and snacks if the child is joining.

### Morning

- leave from your actual base,  
- leave early enough that the drive is believable but not frantic,  
- notice what the family mood is before you arrive.

### During the visit

- watch more than you speak,  
- ask fewer, sharper questions,  
- notice adult energy, transitions, and campus flow,  
- imagine your actual child there, not an easier imaginary version.

### Right after

- do not rush straight into multiple property viewings,
- sit somewhere quiet for 10–20 minutes,
- write your first honest sentence about the day,
- decide what the visit changed.

### One normal task afterwards

Add one ordinary family task if possible:
- lunch,
- groceries,
- a simple drive back,
- or another everyday stop.

That is often where the truth shows up.

## What not to do

- do not stack the day too hard,  
- do not use arrival exhaustion as your only signal,  
- do not leave without notes,  
- do not act like the campus and the commute are separate decisions.

## Pair with

- [Empathy School tour prep](/empathy-school-tour-prep)
- [Empathy School fit notes sheet](/resources/empathy-school-fit-notes-sheet)
- [School tour question list](/resources/school-tour-question-list)

resources.title: Family readiness checklist
resources.description: A copy/paste checklist for deciding whether your family is genuinely ready to test or plan a move to Bali.
resources.body:
## How to use this

Do not use this to pressure yourselves into a yes.
Use it to see whether the move has enough shape to become useful.

Answer each with:
- Yes
- Not yet
- We need to talk about this

---

## Family clarity

- We can say **why** Bali is attractive for our family, not just why it sounds exciting.
- We can say what we are hoping changes in our weekly life.
- We can name the biggest risk or hesitation honestly.
- We know which adult is more ready and which adult still needs clarity.
- We know how our children tend to respond to change, routine shifts, and long days.

## Timeline clarity

- We have a realistic window for a test stay or arrival.
- We know whether we are thinking in weeks, months, or longer.
- We know whether a staged move would feel better than a full commitment.

## Budget clarity

- We have a rough low / mid / high range in mind.
- We are not relying on one perfect housing number.
- We understand that the first month often costs more than later months.

## Area clarity

- We know that choosing an area changes almost everything else.
- We are willing to shortlist two or three areas instead of trying to love all of Bali at once.
- We know what we value most: calmer pace, easier routines, convenience, walkability, school commute, or something else.

## School clarity

- We know whether school needs should shape the move early.
- If Empathy School is in the picture, we are ready to treat it as a real decision anchor rather than a vague idea.
- If school is not the first decision, we know what will anchor the week instead.

## Housing clarity

- We do not expect online listings alone to solve the move.
- We understand that housing gets safer when area and family needs are clearer.
- We are willing to verify before we pay.

## What to do with the result

### If most answers are “Yes”

You probably have enough shape to move into planning mode.
Start here:
- [Plan your move](/plan-your-move)
- [Move timeline](/move-timeline)

### If most answers are “Not yet”

Do not panic.
It usually means the move is still too broad.
Narrow the next step instead of trying to solve everything.

### If the answers are mixed

That is normal.
Choose the one question most likely to reduce the whole family’s uncertainty.
Often that is:
- area,
- timeline,
- budget posture,
- or whether a test stay is the right next move.

## Related

- [Should we move to Bali with kids?](/guides/should-we-move-to-bali-with-kids)
- [Plan your move](/plan-your-move)
- [Move timeline](/move-timeline)
- [Test stay](/test-stay)

resources.title: Rainy day defaults list
resources.description: A short planning list for Bali families who want wet days to feel manageable: indoor options, snack backup, transport backup, dry-clothes plan, and easier evenings.

faqs.q: Why use defaults?
faqs.a: Because wet days are easier when the family does not have to invent a new plan while everyone is already disappointed or tired.

faqs.q: How many defaults do we need?
faqs.a: Usually one indoor option, one snack plan, one transport backup, and one quieter evening version are enough.

faqs.q: Should we cancel everything when it rains?
faqs.a: Not always. The point is simply to know what changes and what stays.

resources.body:
## Copy this into your notes app

### Indoor defaults
- One activity children can do without a long setup.
- One calmer option for a low-energy child.
- One parent-friendly option when adults still need to function.

### Food defaults
- Easy snack ready immediately.
- One warm or comforting meal that does not take much thought.
- Hydration covered before anyone gets grumpy.

### Transport defaults
- Who calls the driver or app?
- What route becomes the backup route?
- What outing is no longer worth it in rain?

### Home defaults
- Where do wet shoes, bags, and towels go?
- Where does laundry dry now?
- Which room becomes the recovery space?

### Evening defaults
- Earlier dinner if the day already feels heavy.
- Lower stimulation.
- Tomorrow prepared in five minutes, not a full reset project.

## Related

- [Rainy season routines in Bali with kids](/guides/rainy-season-routines-in-bali-with-kids)
- [Daily life](/daily-life)
- [Weekday reality planner](/resources/weekday-reality-planner)

resources.title: Sick-day plan for Bali families
resources.description: A parent-first checklist for fever days, stomach bugs, and other rough days in Bali: where to go, what to grab, how to move, and what the rest of the family needs to stop doing.

faqs.q: What belongs on this checklist?
faqs.a: Clinic or hospital route, transport plan, insurance details, comfort basics, fluids, and family role assignments.

faqs.q: Who is this for?
faqs.a: Any family who wants the first sick day in Bali to feel calmer and less improvisational.

faqs.q: Does this replace medical guidance?
faqs.a: No. It helps with preparation and logistics only.

resources.body:
## What this plan should answer in advance

- Who decides whether it is a clinic day or a home day?
- Who handles transport and admin?
- What information do you need immediately?
- What makes the child more comfortable while adults are deciding the next move?

## Keep one simple sick-day protocol

1. Slow the day down.  
2. Check hydration, temperature, and how the child is presenting.  
3. Open the clinic / insurance / location info quickly.  
4. Decide who is with the child and who handles the admin.

## Helpful items to keep ready

- thermometer,
- child medicines you already know how to use,
- electrolytes or hydration support,
- spare clothes,
- charger,
- medical summary note.

## Pair this with

- [Healthcare in Bali for families](/guides/healthcare-in-bali-for-families)
- [Health insurance in Bali for families](/guides/health-insurance-in-bali-for-families)
- [Daily Life](/daily-life)

resources.title: Single-parent stability checklist

resources.body:
## What stability means here

For a single parent, stability usually means the week is small enough, supported enough, and repeatable enough that one hard day does not knock everything over.

## Check the core layers

- area radius,
- transport backup,
- food defaults,
- child anchor,
- adult support or community touchpoints,
- housing that reduces rather than adds friction.

## Strong questions

- If I get sick, what is the backup?
- If transport changes suddenly, what is plan B?
- Does this area still work if I do not have much margin that day?
- Is this school / housing / activity choice making the week lighter or heavier?

resources.title: Weekday reality planner
resources.description: A practical worksheet for pressure-testing a Bali move against the ordinary week: mornings, transport, food, school or camp anchor, after-school rhythm, sick days, and rain.

faqs.q: When should we use this?
faqs.a: Use it before a test stay, during area shortlisting, or when you need to make the first month feel more grounded.

faqs.q: What is the point of this planner?
faqs.a: To stop judging Bali only by highlight moments and test whether ordinary weekdays still work for your family.

faqs.q: Do we need every answer now?
faqs.a: No. The goal is to surface the weak spots early enough to test them honestly.

resources.body:
## Use this planner like a family, not like a school assignment

Write short answers. Be honest. If a question feels annoying, it is probably useful.

### 1. Morning reality
- What time does the family need to be moving?
- What has to happen before that?
- What part of the morning already feels fragile?

### 2. Transport reality
- Which drive matters most?
- How much commute friction can your children really absorb?
- What is your rainy-day backup?

### 3. Food reality
- What are the three breakfasts that always work?
- What is the easy dinner plan on tired days?
- What happens when groceries are not sorted?

### 4. Child anchor
- Is there one repeating anchor this week: school, camp, class, or family routine?
- If not, what would give the child repetition fastest?

### 5. After-school reality
- What happens in the first 45 minutes after pickup?
- Does the child need quiet, movement, or food first?
- What adult task should **not** happen during that window?

### 6. Sick day reality
- Which clinic would you use?
- Who handles transport?
- Where are the important documents?

### 7. Rain reality
- What is the indoor default?
- What part of the day becomes hardest when the weather turns?
- What do you want to simplify on wet days?

- [Weekday reality tool](/weekday-reality)

resources.body:
## Use this checklist for the first 7 days

### Family basics
- [ ] Everyone has enough water, snacks, and simple breakfast options.
- [ ] You know where basic groceries come from.

- [ ] You know where the nearest pharmacy or clinic option is.

- [ ] You have a backup payment method.
- [ ] You saved key addresses in maps.

### Transport
- [ ] You tested the easiest short trip with children.
- [ ] You know whether your family prefers walking, ride-hail, driver, or some combination.
- [ ] You tested one route at a realistic family time, not just the easiest hour.

### Area fit
- [ ] You walked or drove the area in the morning.
- [ ] You checked what late afternoon / evening feels like.
- [ ] You noticed noise, rain drainage, traffic, and family convenience.

- [ ] You are clear whether your current place is just a landing pad or a serious option.
- [ ] If you are viewing homes, you are using a real scorecard rather than memory alone.

- [ ] You protected one familiar ritual from home.

resources.title: Camp questions checklist (copy/paste)
resources.description: A parent-first checklist for choosing camps and short-term programs in Bali—supervision, safety, refunds, communication, and fit.
resources.body:
## Copy/paste questions

### Supervision (the most important section)

- What’s the **adult-to-child ratio** for my child’s age group?
- How do you handle supervision during **transitions** (arrival, bathroom, snack, moving between activities)?
- Who is the “home base” adult my child can return to if they’re overwhelmed?

### Safety + health

- What’s your protocol for **injuries**? (first aid, escalation, when parents are contacted)
- What’s the plan for **illness** (fever, vomiting, etc.)?
- Do you have staff trained in first aid?
- How do you manage **water safety** (if relevant)?

### Allergies + medical needs

- Can you accommodate allergies? What’s the procedure to prevent cross-contact?
- Can you support medication plans (if needed)?
- Who should we inform if a child has sensory needs, anxiety, or support requirements?

### Drop-off / pick-up (security)

- How do you confirm the correct adult is collecting a child?
- What happens if a parent is late?
- Is there a secure handover point (especially for younger kids)?

### Schedule + environment

- What does a typical day look like? (start/end time, indoor/outdoor balance, breaks)
- What do kids do during hot/rainy periods?
- How do you keep kids hydrated and protected from sun?

### Staff quality

- Who are the adults on the ground each day? (teachers, facilitators, assistants)
- How long have they worked with children?
- Who is the point of contact for parents?

### Communication

- How do you communicate with parents (WhatsApp, email, daily notes)?
- Will we get photos or updates—and how often?
- Who do we contact if something feels off?

### Refunds + cancellations

- What is the refund policy if:
  - my child gets sick,
  - we need to change dates,
  - the camp is cancelled,
  - weather disrupts the schedule?
- What exactly is included in the fee (meals, activities, transport)?

### Photos + privacy

- Do you post children publicly on social media?
- How do parents give (or decline) consent?

---

## A calm decision rule

If a camp can’t answer the questions above clearly, it’s usually a sign to:
- choose a shorter commitment, or
- choose a different program.

Clarity beats hype.

resources.title: Culture with kids: quick checklist (Bali)
resources.description: A parent-friendly checklist for joining cultural moments respectfully—without turning them into a performance.

faqs.q: Is this a rulebook?
faqs.a: No. It’s a starting point. When in doubt, ask locals or your community guide and follow their lead.

resources.body:
## Culture with kids (a calm, respectful approach)

This is **experience-based guidance**, not an official authority.
Culture differs by village and context. When in doubt: **ask**, follow local guidance, and stay humble.

### Before you go

- **Ask first:** “Is it okay for us to join/watch?”
- **Dress modestly** (especially for temples/ceremonies): covered shoulders, respectful clothing, and follow local expectations.
- **Keep it simple for kids:** short duration, clear boundaries, snacks/water.
- **Bring a small offering/donation** if your local community suggests it.

### During cultural moments

- **Follow the flow:** stand where others stand, wait when others wait.
- **Don’t treat it like a show:** avoid loud commentary, avoid directing kids like you’re filming.
- **Photos/video:** ask if it’s okay, and avoid filming people closely.
- **Kids first:** if your child is overwhelmed, step out quietly and return later.

### After

- **Debrief gently:** ask kids what they noticed, what felt different, what they liked.
- **Keep it relational:** the goal isn’t “understanding everything,” it’s learning how to be respectful guests.

## Related

- [Daily life](/daily-life)
- [Culture in Bali with kids](/guides/culture-in-bali-with-kids)

resources.description: A copy/paste checklist for your Bali arrival folder—documents and screenshots that reduce stress when you’re tired.

faqs.q: Should we print everything?
faqs.a: You don’t need to print everything, but having a few key pages printed can help if your phone dies or you lose connectivity.

faqs.q: What’s the one thing families forget?
faqs.a: A simple offline note with addresses and emergency contacts.

faqs.q: Where should we confirm the latest entry steps?
faqs.a: Use the official portals and your airline requirements right before travel.

resources.body:
## What belongs in the arrival folder

Keep digital and easy-to-reach copies of:

- passports,
- entry / visa records,
- insurance information,
- school notes,
- housing contacts and agreements,
- payment confirmations,
- driver or transport contacts,
- important addresses.

## Why this matters

The folder is not only for emergencies. It reduces friction in ordinary moments when you are tired and someone asks for one detail you do not want to hunt for.

## Best practice

- One shared digital folder.
- One note with the most-needed numbers and addresses.
- One adult should not be the only person who knows where everything lives.

resources.title: Family budget range planner (low / mid / high)
resources.description: A simple framework to plan a Bali budget range instead of one fragile number.
resources.body:
## Use this worksheet well

This is not a precision spreadsheet. It is a way to stop fragile budgeting.

## Step 1: Build three versions of the month

### Low
What would the month cost if you kept the week intentionally simple?

### Mid
What would it cost if you used the version of Bali you actually want to live, not just the most restrained one?

### High
What would it cost if you added more buffer, support, or convenience?

## Step 2: Fill the four drivers

- housing,
- learning / camps / school-related costs,
- transport,
- daily-life defaults.

## Step 3: Add setup costs separately

Do not hide deposits, short stays, or arrival purchases inside the ordinary monthly number.

## Step 4: Stress-test the budget

Ask:
- Which number still works if the commute is heavier than expected?
- Which number still works if we choose a calmer area but higher rent?
- Which number still works once school becomes part of the week?

## Pair this with

- [Budget calculator](/budget-calculator)
- [Costs](/costs)
- [30-60-90 Bali move board](/resources/30-60-90-bali-move-board)

resources.title: Family transport plan (first month in Bali)
resources.description: A simple worksheet to decide how your family will move around in the first month—walkability, driver use, car needs, and scooter boundaries.

faqs.q: Why plan transport early?
faqs.a: Because transport choices shape your daily stress level more than most families expect.

faqs.q: Do we need scooters?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many families build a great Bali life without scooters.

faqs.q: What’s the calm default?
faqs.a: Walk where possible + driver for longer trips, then reassess once you know your routines.

resources.body:
## What this planner should answer

By the end of the page you should know:

- how the family handles mornings,
- what happens when one adult is unavailable,
- what your backup is in rain or traffic,
- and whether the current area still makes sense once transport is real.

## Build the plan in layers

### Primary plan
Who takes the main school / activity route and how?

### Backup plan
What happens when work runs late, a child is sick, or weather changes the route?

### Tired-day plan
What is the easiest version of the day when nobody has much bandwidth?

## Use transport as a decision signal

If your transport plan keeps getting complicated, the issue may be the area or the housing choice, not your logistics skills.

## Pair this with

- [Commute Reality](/commute-reality)
- [Compare Areas](/compare-areas)
- [Weekday Reality](/weekday-reality)

resources.title: First month in Bali: calm setup checklist
resources.description: A month-one checklist that focuses on calm routines before optimization.
resources.body:
## What this checklist is for

The first month is about making the week lighter, not more ambitious.

## The five categories to set up

### 1. Family paperwork
Passports, entry details, housing notes, school notes, and payment records in one place.

### 2. Transport
A reliable way to get to the first few repeated commitments.

### 3. Food + home defaults
Breakfast, groceries, water, laundry, and one or two low-decision dinners.

### 4. Child rhythm
Sleep, after-school decompression, one weekly anchor, and a rain backup.

### 5. Adult bandwidth
One way to reduce planning fatigue: shared note, calendar, budget tracker, or clearer division of admin.

## Keep asking

- What is still too hard every week?
- What can become more repeatable?
- What decision are we postponing that actually needs attention now?

## Pair this with

- [First Month Planner](/first-month-planner)
- [Weekday Reality](/weekday-reality)

resources.title: Lease + deposit checklist (copy/paste questions)
resources.description: Use this checklist before paying a deposit or signing a lease in Bali—clarity now prevents stress later.

faqs.q: Is this legal advice?
faqs.a: No. It’s a practical checklist to help you ask better questions and get clarity in writing.

faqs.q: Should we use an agent?
faqs.a: Some families do. Whether you do or not, always verify details and avoid rushing payments.

faqs.q: What matters most?
faqs.a: Payment schedule, what’s included, and how deposits are returned.

resources.body:
## Copy/paste questions

### People + authority
- Who is the owner / authorized signer?
- Can you show proof of authority to rent this property?

### Money
- Total rent amount and currency
- Payment schedule (monthly / quarterly / yearly)
- Deposit amount and what it covers
- How deposit return is calculated and when it’s returned

### What’s included
- Electricity included? If not, how is it billed?
- Water included?
- Internet included and what speed/provider?
- Pool/garden maintenance included?
- Cleaning included?

### Maintenance
- Who fixes what?
- Typical response time?
- What happens if internet/power is unreliable?

### Exit + disputes
- Early exit policy
- What happens if there’s a dispute?
- Who is the contact person?
